0b10c537d622eaed: SINGAPORE: Asian stocks slipped on Friday and were poised for a second straight weekly drop as investors fretted about elevated energy prices, bond market ructions and the huge sums needed to fund AI investment.

Brent crude futures were at US$103.70 per barrel in Asian hours after surging more than 4 per cent in the previous session on concerns over the war in the Middle East that has fanned inflation worries and led to higher rates across the globe.

President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before November's US midterm elections, although traders remained sceptical of any progress being made to end the war.
"The big question for markets is whether Trump sticks to his word if Iranian attacks intensify," said Nick Twidale, chief market strategist at ATFX Global.

"Any indication that the White House is reconsidering military action could see oil prices spike sharply higher, particularly with tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz already under significant pressure."

In stocks, MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was down 0.16 per cent, set for an over 1 per cent drop for the week. Markets in South Korea and Taiwan were closed for a holiday. Japan's Nikkei fell more than 1 per cent.
Tech stocks led Wall Street's main indexes lower overnight after a report that OpenAI's annualised revenue was US$20 billion less than the company previously signalled hit sentiment.

"It has been a sea of red across technology, AI infrastructure and semiconductors, with the OpenAI headlines seemingly providing the catalyst for investors to take some exposure off the table," said Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone.

"For now, though, the price action suggests investors are becoming more selective about where they want exposure and, importantly, what price they are prepared to pay for future growth," he said in a note.
BOND BINGE FOR AI
Investors were also weighing a massive round of fundraising that appears to be on the way, with SpaceX, Broadcom and Oracle all expected to raise billions to buy high-end AI chips.

Australia's Firmus, a data centre operator backed by Nvidia , shelved its US$5 billion initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions, and said it would opt for a private fundraising round instead.

A toxic mix of higher energy costs, expectations of central bank interest rate hikes and concerns over rising government debts have fuelled a months-long global bond selloff, pushing borrowing costs to multi-decade highs.

"With long-term yields back around multi-decade highs, investors no longer have the luxury of valuing AI growth in a low-cost-of-capital world," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo.

Chanana said higher sovereign yields and now rising corporate issuance to fund AI infrastructure mean capital is becoming "both more expensive and more selective, which puts balance sheets and the quality of future earnings firmly in focus."
FOCUS REMAINS ON FRANCE
France has been hit particularly hard as investors scrutinise its debt load, budget deficit and political outlook ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

"With the two rounds of the presidential elections only in April and May next year, French bond spreads are still looking at more than half a year of higher volatility and continued spread elevation," ING analysts said in a note.

US Treasury markets have been calmer as solid auctions this week helped the mood somewhat. The benchmark 10-year yield was steady at 5.226 per cent but was not far from the 24-year high it hit on Wednesday.
"It does not mean the bond market sell-off is over, but it does at least put it on pause, at least just for now," ING analysts said.

In currencies, the dollar stood tall as the euro was set for a fifth straight week in the red. It last fetched US$1.122, straddling the 17-month low it touched earlier this week on French debt worries.

ffe4fd036eb306fc: NEW YORK, Oct 9 — New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said yesterday he would ask US President Donald Trump to remove federal immigration agents from the city as tensions flared over the latest shooting involving ICE.
The New York Police Department said a man had been shot around 4:00 pm in the Marble Hill neighbourhood of the Bronx during an altercation with federal agents.

Mamdani and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) later confirmed that the shooting occurred during an operation of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the agency responsible for Trump’s immigration crackdown.

A DHS spokesman said in a statement that agents were attempting to “to arrest a criminal illegal alien from the Dominican Republic with a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession.”
It did not state how many officers fired their weapons or why.
“ICE officers immediately rendered aid. The individual is alive and at a local hospital,” the DHS spokesman said.
The department initially claimed that the person targeted had associations with a Dominican gang, but later issued a revised statement removing that sentence.
Mamdani said that a five-year-old child was in the car when the altercation occurred.
“This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation,” the Democratic mayor said on X, adding that he had called the president.
“When we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities,” he added.
Trump, a Republican, heavily criticized Mamdani before he took office in January, but the two men have since struck a surprisingly warm relationship.
Several hundred protesters gathered peacefully at the scene of the shooting yesterday evening to express opposition to Trump’s crackdown, AFP observed.
Many people then moved to the nearby hospital where the victim was being treated.
Tensions with the police escalated when some protesters attempted to prevent cars from leaving the hospital, before being moved away from the entrance by law enforcement, who set up barriers.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul posted to X yesterday, saying she expects “federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident.”
“This incident is another reminder of the unchecked, rampant violence ICE has been spreading throughout our communities,” said Murad Awawdeh, president of the New York Immigration Coalition.
“We demand an immediate investigation into the shooting, the release of the body camera footage, and accountability for any ICE agents who used excessive force.”
ICE has been involved in several high-profile shootings this year, including the killing of two US citizens in Minneapolis, which sparked angry protests.
New York, a Democratic stronghold, is one of several US cities that bars its police force from assisting with federal immigration enforcement. — AFP

The ministry said El-Sisi is also scheduled to meet Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim to assess progress in bilateral cooperation and exchange views on regional and international issues of mutual interest.
Both leaders will witness the exchange of memoranda of understanding between Malaysia and Egypt, followed by an official high tea at the Seri Perdana Complex hosted by the prime minister.
In 2025, Egypt was Malaysia's seventh largest trading partner in Africa.
Malaysia's total trade with Egypt was valued at RM3.08 billion (US$0.72 billion), with exports at RM2.55 billion (US$0.60 billion) and imports at RM0.53 billion (US$0.12 billion).
From January to August, total trade between the two countries increased by 74.7 per cent to RM3.49 billion (US$0.87 billion).

1239c3fdd85e46c1: WASHINGTON, Oct 9 — OpenAI is bringing in about US$20 billion (RM82 billion) less in annualised revenue than investors had been led to believe, the Financial Times reported yesterday, raising questions about the solidity of the AI business.
Citing documents shared with OpenAI’s financial backers, the FT said the company put its annualised revenue at close to US$50 billion as of the end of September.
Media reports late last month had pegged the figure at US$70 billion based on information given to investors.

Investors track annualised revenue at OpenAI and Anthropic as the clearest signal of demand for artificial intelligence, and the figures help justify enormous spending on data centres as well as the AI-fuelled stock market rally.

The metric, which tech startups commonly use to signal their growth trajectory, is sometimes criticised as imprecise or even misleading, since it typically extrapolates a single month’s sales across a full year.

In an apparent pushback, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC that the earlier number, which the network reported as US$68 billion, counted gross revenue from OpenAI’s partnerships with companies like chipmaker Nvidia.
That method was intended to make it easier for investors to measure the company against chief rival Anthropic.
The report weighed on AI-linked stocks, with Nvidia down 2.9 per cent, SpaceX down 4 per cent and Oracle losing nearly 6 per cent.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to AFP’s request for comment.
The report lands as OpenAI negotiates a fresh private fundraising that could value it at roughly US$1.4 trillion, according to the FT.
OpenAI, which confidentially submitted paperwork for an initial public offering in June, had been widely expected to go public this fall, but it has since pushed back the listing.
Archrival Anthropic is expected to list on the public markets next month. — AFP

c477600cbb5ba2c1: TAWAU, Oct 9 — Police arrested 14 male students yesterday in connection with a group student fight involving weapons at the Taman Ambar Playground, Jalan Kuhara here last Monday.

Tawau District Police Chief ACP Rosdi Mat Jusoh said the Criminal Investigation Division of the Tawau District Police Headquarters detained the suspects, aged between 12 and 14, to assist with the investigation.

“Police received a report regarding the fight at 6pm last Monday. Preliminary investigations found that the incident stemmed from a misunderstanding between two students before a fight broke out, which subsequently involved several other students.

“A viral video recording of the incident also helped police identify the individuals and their respective roles. In addition, police seized a mobile phone and a black bicycle believed to be related to the investigation,” he said in a statement here today.
He added that the case is being investigated under Section 148 of the Penal Code and Section 6(1)(c) of the Immigration Act 1959/63.

“Investigations are underway to determine the involvement and role of each arrested individual. Furthermore, the police are obtaining original video recordings, as well as recording statements from witnesses and the detainees.
“At the same time, the police are also awaiting the victim’s medical report and cooperating with the school authorities and the Tawau District Education Office regarding the case,” he added.

Rosdi urged members of the public who witnessed the incident or possess any related information to come forward and assist with the investigation by contacting the investigating officer, Insp Robiatul Adawiyah Japri, at 016-918 9402 or by visiting the nearest police station.
In the meantime, he reminded the public that any act of rioting, attacking others, or using any object as a weapon is a serious offence that will not be compromised.

“Parents and guardians are advised to monitor their children’s associations and behaviour, while students are reminded not to get involved in fights, provoke others, or join groups that could lead to criminal behaviour,” he said. — Bernama
58400b8d49977efb: OCTOBER 9 — By shifting our focus from victim-blaming to conversational analysis, we can dismantle the coercive scripts behind financial fraud.

“You should have been more careful.” “Foolish people lose money like that.” “Uneducated.” “Greedy.” “Use your brain.” These are the harsh words scam victims often hear after losing their money. Instead of receiving sympathy and support, they are frequently blamed for what happened to them.

But before we point a finger at a scam victim, we should pause and ask: Was the victim really making decisions in a neutral state of mind? In almost every case, the answer is no. A scam phone call suddenly confronts a person with intense fear, artificial urgency, aggressive authority, and uncertainty. Under severe emotional pressure, critical thinking degrades. By the time the victim realizes something is wrong, the money is already gone leaving behind deep financial loss, embarrassment, and trauma.

Telling a victim “You should have known better” does not recover lost funds. Calling someone “stupid” does not prevent the next crime. Victim blaming simply silences people, keeping critical scam patterns hidden.

This brings us to a far more important question: Why do even educated, careful, and experienced people fall for scams? To answer this, we must look beyond the victim and examine what the scammer is actually doing. Scammers are not merely people who lie, they deliberately construct conversations engineered to manipulate how a person thinks, feels, and responds. In other words, scams are linguistic events. And if scammers know how to weaponize language against us, we can use linguistic analysis to recognise and break their tactics.
A police officer stands beside the National Scam Response Centre logo at Menara 2 MCMC in Cyberjaya, Selangor on March 3, 2026. — Picture by Yusof Isa

Simulated authority (impersonation): Scammers frequently impersonate police officers, government officials, bank managers, or tax agents. By adopting formal language, precise administrative titles, and local details, such as “I’m Aida, inspector from IPD Muar, Johor, and we need your address and IC to double-confirm your information,” they exploit our natural tendency to respect authority. The formal phrases and explicit local references make the call sound authentic, even though sounding official is not the same as being official.

Manufactured urgency: Scammers want victims to act before they have time to verify facts or consult family. When a scammer claims that “…SKMM is to bar all your lines and might blacklist you,” the conversation shifts from a standard inquiry to an immediate crisis. Driven by fear of severe disruption, victims focus on solving the perceived threat rather than checking if the threat is genuine.

Enforced isolation: A critical instruction in many scam scripts is “Do not discuss this matter with anyone.” While framed as official confidentiality, its real objective is isolation. A third party, a colleague, relative, or friend, can easily interrupt the scammer’s narrative by asking simple, objective questions. Secrecy keeps the victim trapped in the scammer’s psychological grip.

Weaponized fear: Scammers use legal threats to induce panic. Statements like “This enquiry could cause actions to be taken against you legally under the Official Secrets Act,” are delivered not to inform, but to terrify. Words like legal action, blacklist, arrest, and penalty carry heavy psychological weight. Delivered in a calm, authoritative tone, they effectively paralyze critical judgment.

When a victim loses money, they lose far more than a figure on a bank statement. They lose months or years of hard work, time, and security saved for retirement, education, or healthcare. Preventing these losses requires a fundamental shift in how society responds.

Instead of asking victim-blaming questions like “How could you be so foolish?” or “Why didn’t you use your brain?”, we must start asking diagnostic questions: “What did the scammer say?” and “How did they make you feel?”

Sharing scam experiences provides crucial intelligence. When victims report hearing similar phrases, threats, and instructions, those linguistic patterns become public knowledge that can protect others. Recognizing the warning signs, demands for immediate action, threats of legal arrest, instructions for secrecy, and hyper-formal language allows potential victims to pause, verify, and stay safe.
The fight against financial fraud is not only about banking security or legal enforcement, but also about language. Scammers weaponize language; by analyzing it, we break their code.
* Tamilhiile Manggai G Mohgan is a language lecturer at the Faculty of Languages and Linguistics, Universiti Malaya, and may be reached at tamilhiilemanggai@um.edu.my
** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
56746aed7e41cec1: During the height of the Covid-19 pandemic, as global attention focused heavily on the economic fallout and job losses, director Ekien Zainal found herself drawn to a quieter, darker tragedy unfolding behind closed doors: the intense psychological strain on locked-down families.
That unsettling reality inspired 'Miselia', a telefilm exploring trauma, identity disorders and the fragile state of human nature under extreme isolation.
"I didn't just think about the people who lost their jobs," Ekien says following a recent preview of the movie at RTM Angkasapuri.
"I wondered about families — wives and children overwhelmed by constant problems. The pressure back then was intense. That idea grew into a full script."
The project underwent several title shifts, originally named 'Logamaya' and 'Fatamorgana'.
"'Miselia' is a fictional word I made up, inspired by the scientific term mycelium, referring to the fine network of threads that forms a fungus."
The main character attempts to support her household by cultivating small mushroom beds.
Mushrooms serve as a central symbol in the drama of the blurring of reality and illusion.
"If you look closely, you see mushrooms releasing spores," Ekien says.
"In real life, spores are active in the morning, but in the film, it happens at noon.
"That is part of the character's hallucinations. It is a way for the audience to understand the different personalities inside the house."

To heighten the eerie atmosphere, Ekien filmed at Fraser's Hill and created a fictional setting called Valmont Hill, complete with custom street signs, to keep the dark narrative distinct from real locations.
The director had high praise for the ensemble cast, which includes Ellie Suriaty, Azhar Sulaiman, Niezam Zaidi, Adam Shahz and Shiqin Kamal.
"I give them six out of five stars. Every actor gave a dedicated performance that gave me goosebumps.
"The production crew also poured their hearts into the project to ensure top quality."
'Miselia' premieres on Oct 10 on TV1 and will be available for streaming on RTMKlik.
bf99e9dde6864222: TANJONG KARANG: A father is struggling to come to terms with the loss of his eldest daughter and two grandchildren in a road crash involving a multi-purpose vehicle (MPV) and a lorry at Bukit Talang, Jalan Raja Musa, yesterday.

Mat Talpi Salamat, 72, said he rushed to the scene after receiving a call from his fifth child, Norhaslinda, 34, informing him that his eldest daughter, Norawalysa, 44, had been involved in the crash at about 1.30pm.

The grocery store owner arrived to find his grandchildren, Auni Syazana Suhaimi, 12, and Ahmad Syah Fawwaz Suhaimi, 8, lying at the scene, while firefighters worked to free Norawalysa, who was trapped in the vehicle.
Another grandchild, Ahmad Syah Fitri, 10, who was also in the MPV, sustained head injuries.
Recalling the tragedy at Masjid Darul Iman in Kampung Parit Serong last night, Mat Talpi fought back tears as he described seeing his grandchildren at the scene.
"When I arrived, I saw my grandchildren lying there, while firefighters were extricating their mother.
"Seeing that there was no hope, I kissed them right there. How can I forget them when they loved me so much?" he said.
Mat Talpi said he had last seen Norawalysa and her family the previous week, when they shared a meal of fried noodles prepared by her.

"I never imagined she and her children would leave us like this. She was my eldest child and an exemplary sibling. She was friendly and always willing to help. It is hard for our family to accept this trial," he said.
Norhaslinda said she noticed a change in her sister's demeanour during the family gathering the previous week.
"She usually talked a lot, but that day she was mostly silent. Only after she passed away did I realise it was a sign she would be leaving us forever," she said.
Norhaslinda said her sister had helped her greatly, particularly with career guidance and financial support.
Norawalysa and her two children were buried in a single grave at the Kampung Parit Serong Islamic Cemetery at 1am today.
The three died after their Proton Exora MPV crashed into the rear of a lorry yesterday afternoon.
Initial police investigations found that the lorry had pulled over onto the left shoulder of the road due to a flat tyre.
The case is being investigated under Section 41(1) of the Road Transport Act 1987.

300bd35aa063e78c: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia has retained its Tier 2 ranking in the 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report released by the United States Department of State, marking the third consecutive year it has held the rating.
The Home Ministry said the ranking reflected continued international recognition of Malaysia's sustained efforts to combat human trafficking.

The report acknowledged the country's progress, including stronger law enforcement, prosecutions of public officials complicit in trafficking crimes and increased government funding for anti-trafficking operations.

Other measures included a significant increase in specialised officers, particularly in Sabah and Sarawak, and amendments to two regulations under the Anti-Trafficking in Persons and Anti-Smuggling of Migrants Act 2007 to improve the duration of permissions granted under the law.

The ministry also cited related amendments concerning extended protection orders and the management of victims whose extended protection orders had expired, as well as the opening of new shelters operated by non-governmental organisations.

Enforcement capacity in Sabah and Sarawak had also been strengthened, with operations targeting high-risk sectors such as oil palm plantations and rubber glove manufacturing, it said in a statement today.
Malaysia retained its Tier 2 ranking in the 2025 report after receiving the same rating in 2024.
In 2023, the country was placed on the Tier 2 Watch List, with its last Tier 2 rating before 2024 in 2017.
The ministry said the 2026 report also outlined eight recommendations for Malaysia to implement during the next assessment period, from April 1 this year to March 31 next year.

Among the key recommendations were strengthening early victim identification mechanisms, improving the quality of case investigations, eliminating recruitment fees charged to workers and expanding strategic partnerships with NGOs.
In response, the government has outlined several strategies, including strengthening the integrity of public servants and establishing a victim management system in line with international standards.
The ministry said the government would also strengthen cooperation with civil society organisations and NGOs, while making greater use of digital technology and artificial intelligence.

The ministry added that the Council for Anti-Trafficking in Persons and Anti-Smuggling of Migrants (MAPO), which it leads alongside other government agencies, was committed to implementing coordinated measures to address emerging trends, including job scams.
Combating human trafficking requires close cooperation among various parties through a holistic approach centred on enforcement and legislation, victim protection and prevention, it said.

"The government is confident that this comprehensive approach would strengthen efforts to combat human trafficking, bring offenders to justice, uphold human rights and protect victims, while safeguarding public order and national security."
05ec507657e47c18: LOS ANGELES, Oct 9 — John Cena spent much of his childhood playing with Matchbox cars, so when the chance came to hit the gas in “Matchbox: The Movie,” he jumped behind the wheel.

The action-comedy film, out this Friday on Apple TV, follows the reunion of a group of childhood friends – a gathering that veers unexpectedly when they’re caught in the middle of a wild mission to recover a nuclear warhead.
Starring Cena, Jessica Biel, Arturo Castro, Sam Richardson and Teyonah Parris, the movie directed by Sam Hargrave melds high-octane scenes with more humorous moments.

It also taps into nostalgia for the toy cars, which originated after English engineer Jack Odell designed the first model to comply with a 1952 British school rule requiring toys to fit inside a matchbox.

“If you have childhood memories like me of Matchbox, I think you’re going to appreciate all the Easter eggs in there. And if you don’t know anything about Matchbox or the Mattel franchise, you’re going to sit down and really enjoy this movie,” Cena said during a roundtable with journalists.
The action scenes proved difficult for both Cena and his co-star Biel.
Training focused more on learning to move in new ways, and doing fight scenes with greater fluidity, Cena said.
And, of course, to “gain the courage to jump off a building,” he added.
Adrenaline rush
Biel said it was the driving that propelled her out of her comfort zone.
“I’ve never learned how to spin a car, you know, in a 180 and stop it on a mark,” she said.
The experience proved an adrenaline rush, Biel added.

Driving “was the coolest stuff I got to do,” she said. “Going 60 plus miles an hour on a freeway with a bunch of camera cars everywhere, and guys on motorcycles, and gals in giant semis... There was a really major sense of being safe for everyone else’s sake.”
Given the demanding action scenes, both actors said the direction of Hargrave was crucial.
The filmmaker is known for his stunt work and coordination on Marvel Cinematic Universe films.
“He was such a big draw to this movie because of his experience and his expertise in the stunt world, and how he likes to do things practically,” Biel said.
For the actors it was also an opportunity to reflect on the importance of friendship, and to share stories from behind the wheel.
Cena, who is himself a car collector, recounted one of the most significant car purchases of his life — “a fake Lamborghini.”
He bought the vehicle on the cheap with the intention of fixing it up himself. Ultimately he blew US$825,000 and two decades of work on the venture in vain.
But he learned a valuable life lesson.
“If you think it’s too good to be true,”he said, “it’s too good to be true.” — AFP

c9f35f5c02fd263c: RIYADH, Oct 9 — The Saudi civil defence agency said a kindergarten and a medical complex in Riyadh were damaged by debris from a missile interception yesterday, as Yemen’s Houthis announced attacks targeting the capital’s airport.
Two witnesses said that a plane at the airport belonging to national flag carrier Saudia had cracks and holes in its fuselage. A source briefed on the matter said three planes suffered damage.

Saudi Arabia leads a pro-government coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen’s civil war. The Iran-backed group has repeatedly targeted Riyadh since the conflict roared back to life in July, vowing to hit critical infrastructure and disrupt Saudi airspace.
The scale and frequency of the attacks on the Saudi capital have been unprecedented in the eight months of wider war in the Middle East.

The Houthis announced three attacks yesterday against Riyadh airport. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group also launched missiles at an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
Recent attacks have also targeted oil infrastructure in the world’s largest crude exporter.
The Houthis yesterday warned workers to evacuate Saudi Arabia’s oil facilities, having days before hit a major refinery south of the capital.
Earlier in the day, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted two missiles fired towards Riyadh.
The kingdom’s civil defence agency said “interception debris” had damaged a kindergarten and a medical complex in the city. It did not say if there were casualties or provide details of the damage.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of civilian targets being hit are relatively rare. There have been few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.
Shelter in place
After resuming their fight against Yemen’s internationally recognised government following a four-year lull, the Houthis last month seized all of the country’s Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive.

The group, whose heartlands are among the Zaidi Shia Muslims in the northwest, had already controlled the capital Sanaa and most of Yemen’s major population centres since the start of the war in 2014. Riyadh’s military coalition intervened in 2015 to support the government.

Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces have struggled to roll back the Houthis’ advance, despite an ambitious counter-offensive aimed at recapturing territory, including the area around a crucial sea route for global energy flows.
In Riyadh, diplomats were instructed to shelter at their respective embassies, some of them told AFP, after explosions echoed around the city yesterday morning.
There were no text alerts warning residents, as there had been in the past.

An interior ministry campaign has repeatedly warned residents against sharing unauthorised information, images or footage of missiles, drones and their impacts, warning that violators of legal consequences.
Several residents told AFP that international schools were taking precautions, with at least one facility sending children into a basement for safety.
“My daughter called me,” one parent told AFP on condition of anonymity, saying she was “completely distraught”.
Two people working in Riyadh’s business hub, the King Abdullah Financial District, told AFP that some companies were evacuating staff from the area.
‘Heightened vigilance’
Numerous flights at Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport were delayed or cancelled, according to information posted for passengers.
The airport did not immediately acknowledge disruption, pointing only in a short statement to the “necessity” of contacting airlines before travelling.
The United States urged its citizens in Saudi Arabia to “exercise heightened vigilance” following the attacks at the airport, which US government employees now need “special authorisation” to use.
Previous attacks killed a Sudanese national at Riyadh airport, as well as an Egyptian and an Algerian national at Abha airport, civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday.
In Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, civilians are paying the price for the renewed fighting, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.
A humanitarian crisis caused by the war has left most of the nation’s population dependent on aid.
After declaring its counter-offensive, Yemen’s government claimed to have pushed Houthi fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea coast and the port city of Mocha.
But the Houthis insist they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides have not reported any major changes on the ground.
The rival claims have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.

The Houthis recently seized areas south of Taiz, Yemen’s third largest city, cutting it off from the government’s temporary capital in Aden and sparking shortages and soaring prices for food and energy. — AFP
94d7a4f4b56f93f7: SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 9 — Anthropic on Thursday moved to bar users from treating its Claude AI system with needless cruelty, amid a growing philosophical debate over whether artificial intelligence can be conscious.
The San Francisco-based AI lab updated its usage policy to include “a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behaviour toward our models.”
“Claude’s ability to end these interactions will remain the primary enforcement mechanism,” the policy states.

The updated policy does not explicitly cite so-called “model welfare,” the idea that AI systems might deserve types of protection usually reserved for living things, but Anthropic and its executives have openly entertained the concept.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Already last year, the company said it was giving Claude the ability to end conversations in rare, extreme cases of “persistently harmful or abusive user interactions.”
Then in February, CEO Dario Amodei told The New York Times he was unsure whether AI models could be conscious.
“We don’t know if the models are conscious...But we’re open to the idea that it could be,” Amodei said.

Science fiction and popular culture have been fascinated for decades by the boundary between technology and human intelligence, but asking whether AI is conscious may be the wrong question, according to Jackson Stakeman, a general manager at Sparq, an Atlanta-based AI services provider.
“Consciousness is a trap. We can’t prove it in each other. Debate it for AI and you go in circles,” Stakeman told AFP.
“The mirror is a better metaphor. These systems reflect what we put in, at scale. That’s reason enough for the policy change” at Anthropic, he added.
Some have rejected the idea of machine consciousness outright, including Pope Leo XIV and Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman.
“AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer,” Suleyman wrote in an essay last month.
“Granting rights and moral protections to a technological entity, one that looks to be on a path to be seismically more capable and intelligent than us, is a recipe for disaster,” he wrote.
In a sermon delivered in Italian on Thursday at St. Peter’s Basilica in Vatican City, the pope suggested machines lack a soul, saying they merely “compile data” quickly.
“The mind must not simply compile data – as an algorithm now does more quickly than we can,” the pontiff said.
It must “recall lived experiences, which contain depths of meaning that only the human soul can recognise, and connect more deeply with the goodness of these experiences,” the pope said. — AFP
d071cabe4c483b92: NEW YORK, Oct 9 — The United States yesterday filed new torture charges against ousted Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, bolstering a mounting criminal case against the pair held in US custody.
Maduro and Flores already face drug trafficking and firearms charges in the United States after they were snatched from their Caracas compound in an extraordinary US military raid in January.

A new court filing shows both are now further charged with conspiracy to commit torture against victims, including US citizens, in Venezuelan detention — with prosecutors detailing alleged waterboardings, rapes and beatings.
Torture was allegedly used to “intimidate, harass, and neutralize their opponents, including through kidnappings.”
In a 2022 instance, Venezuelan authorities allegedly tortured an American who they accused of plotting to assassinate Maduro.

“That torture included electric shock to arms, legs, and genitals; asphyxiation; beatings; deprivation of food and water; and forced injections of a substance that caused (the victim) to experience seizures,” the filing states.
During his 2013-2026 presidency, rights groups widely accused Maduro of using political repression to cling to power.

“These additional charges reflect the dedication of this Administration to delivering justice for the victims of torture, narcoterrorism, and organized crime,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said on X.
FBI Director Kash Patel said the latest charges showed Washington’s commitment to “accountability, the rule of law, and the protection of US national security.”
‘Prisoner of war’
Maduro and Flores are slated for a trial in New York next June and are being held in a Brooklyn jail.
US prosecutors claim that Maduro used state power to protect and promote illegal drug smuggling, and that he allied himself with cartels to ship tons of cocaine into the United States.

Maduro has denied the charges he originally faced: “narco-terrorism” conspiracy, cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices as well as conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
He has described himself as a “prisoner of war” and said the US military kidnapped him.
Flores has similarly pleaded not guilty to cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
She has been additionally charged with “narco-terrorism” conspiracy, the court filing showed.
Also yesterday, a US court denied a request by Flores to be moved from jail to private home detention in New York to help her address an apparent heart problem.
The pair have both appealed to have the charges against them dismissed, claiming they have immunity as president and first lady of a sovereign country.
Since Maduro’s capture, vice-president Delcy Rodriguez has governed Venezuela as interim leader under intense pressure from US President Donald Trump’s administration.
US energy firms have this year signed a raft of multi-billion-dollar deals with Venezuela, which has agreed to grant the United States control of a huge chunk of its vast oil reserves. — AFP

ebf5270ffc508033: From Chang Lih Kang
In June, the science, technology and innovation ministry said in a parliamentary reply that it was leading the government’s efforts to develop a National Technology Sovereignty Framework.
But what does technology sovereignty mean to everyday Malaysians, when almost every chip, cloud service and line of code we depend on comes from elsewhere?

It does not mean producing everything ourselves. It means having the choice and control over critical technologies, data and infrastructure so that no external party can unilaterally dictate our options.

If geopolitical tensions disrupt supply chains, Malaysia must have alternatives. If a major cyber incident occurs, our hospitals, banks, businesses and government systems must continue operating. We also need the expertise and institutions to decide how emerging technologies should be adopted and governed.
Ultimately, technology sovereignty protects Malaysia’s freedom of choice in the digital world.

The Huawei episode illustrates why this matters. Washington restricted Huawei’s access to US technology, including advanced semiconductors, and urged allies to reconsider Chinese equipment in their 5G networks. Dependence is not simply about whether we can afford technology, but whether we can still access it when geopolitical circumstances change.

Taiwan offers another lesson. Its semiconductor industry, led by companies such as TSMC, sits at the heart of global advanced-chip production. Yet this concentration also creates vulnerabilities, as industries worldwide depend on a relatively small number of facilities.

I am not arguing against globalisation. Global supply chains have brought Malaysia investment, jobs, technology transfer and access to markets. But being connected to the world is not the same as being resilient to it.

South Korea demonstrates how sustained investment in strategic capabilities can strengthen technological independence. By developing its semiconductor, electronics and manufacturing industries, it has produced global leaders such as Samsung and SK Hynix, including in memory chips critical to advanced artificial intelligence systems.

India offers a different model. Its digital public infrastructure, including digital identity and payment platforms, gives it greater control over key parts of its digital economy. It is also investing in semiconductor design, manufacturing and packaging. Its experience shows that sovereignty does not require complete self-sufficiency, but strategic capabilities in selected areas.

China has built domestic strengths across telecommunications, cloud computing, payments and artificial intelligence. Yet it continues to face challenges in producing the most advanced semiconductors and accessing sophisticated chipmaking equipment. Even a country with enormous resources cannot quickly replace every critical technology when external access is restricted.

For countries such as Malaysia, dependence without alternatives carries serious consequences. Wars, sanctions, export controls and corporate decisions can disrupt access to technology, components and digital infrastructure. Having the money to buy something does not guarantee that we can obtain it.

Malaysia starts from a relatively strong position. We have more than 50 years of experience in electronics and semiconductors, established industrial clusters in Penang and Kulim, and account for around 13% of global chip assembly, testing and packaging. We are also the world’s sixth-largest semiconductor exporter.

However, much of this capacity operates within multinational facilities. We host significant production, but need to build greater locally owned capabilities. Advanced packaging, increasingly important for AI chips, is one area where Malaysia must strengthen its position.
Our research base also needs improvement. Gross expenditure on research and development stands at around 1% of gross domestic product, compared with a much higher share in South Korea.
These gaps expose Malaysia to four key risks.
First, security: critical government and infrastructure systems must remain operational during geopolitical tensions, cyberattacks and technological disruptions.
Second, economic resilience: disruptions to semiconductors, cloud services or network equipment could affect manufacturing, finance, healthcare, logistics and communications.
Third, data governance: sensitive government, health, financial and commercial data must be managed in accordance with Malaysian law and national interests.

Fourth, competitiveness: countries that develop technological capabilities capture more value through intellectual property, skilled employment, research, start-ups and globally competitive companies. Those that mainly consume technology capture less.

The framework should therefore identify technologies where excessive dependence could threaten Malaysia’s security, economy or ability to govern. In these areas, we should build domestic capabilities, diversify suppliers, maintain strategic reserves where appropriate and establish trusted partnerships.
Elsewhere, we should remain open.

Technology sovereignty is not protectionism, economic nationalism or a retreat from the global economy. Foreign investment, multinational companies and international research partnerships have contributed enormously to Malaysia’s development. We must continue welcoming their capital, expertise, technology and access to global markets.
Our goal is not to own everything. It is to ensure that Malaysia cannot be held hostage by dependence on anything critical to its security, economy and future.
As technology becomes increasingly intertwined with our daily lives, the ability to make independent choices will matter more than ever.

Malaysia’s digital future should not simply be something we take for granted. We must build the capabilities to shape it, the resilience to protect it and the sovereignty to decide our own path forward.
Chang Lih Kang is the science, technology, and innovation minister
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
b987e0a67c35e51c: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 9 — Borrowers facing difficulties settling their National Higher Education Fund Corporation (PTPTN) loan arrears are welcomed to come forward to negotiate for loan restructuring or apply for deferment according to permitted flexibilities.

4bfc7a75c4540df1: PARIS, Oct 9 — Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka has been fined 150,000 Swiss francs (RM737,000) after admitting using a forged Covid vaccine certificate during the pandemic when he played for Arsenal.
The 34-year-old Sunderland skipper will not have to pay the fine provided he commits no further offences during a two-year probationary period.

“I was sentenced by summary judgment for obtaining a false certification to a suspended fine of 50 daily rates of 3,000 Swiss francs each with a two-year probationary period,” he wrote in German on Instagram.
“I accept the decision and take responsibility for my actions. Thank you for the many messages of support over the past few weeks. They mean a lot to me.”
Xhaka was playing for Arsenal at the time in 2022 before moving to Bayern Leverkusen the following year and joining Sunderland in 2025.
Switzerland’s most capped player with 152 appearances, Xhaka withdrew from their Nations League matches against Scotland, North Macedonia and Slovenia in the recent international break.
On Monday, Xhaka admitted that he had presented a forged certificate to avoid mandatory vaccination during the Covid crisis.
“At the time, I was very worried about the issue of Covid-19 vaccination... I felt deep mistrust regarding the vaccine and was gripped by anxiety and doubt,” he said on Instagram.
“Today I clearly see that I made the wrong choice. It was a mistake. I am sorry,” he wrote, adding that he was “cooperating fully with the relevant authorities”.
Switzerland are subsequently set to face Slovenia on November 13 and Scotland on November 16, also as part of the Nations League. — AFP

e81932742b4f792c: SAN ISIDRO, Oct 9 — Argentine prosecutors argued yesterday that the “chaotic” medical team treating football legend Diego Maradona at the time of his death should receive prison sentences up to 12 years.
Seven medical professionals have been on trial since April over Maradona’s death on November 25, 2020 while convalescing after surgery for a brain clot.

The star of the 1986 World Cup died of heart failure and acute pulmonary edema — a condition where fluid accumulates in the lungs — at a rented home in the Buenos Aires suburb of Tigre two weeks after going under the knife.
The larger-than-life star, who had a history of substance abuse, was 60 at the time of his death.
His medical team, including his chief doctor, psychiatrist, psychologist and nurses, are accused of providing grossly inadequate care in the lead-up to his death. They deny the charges.
In his closing arguments, prosecutor Patricio Ferrai said the defendants’ “chaotic organisation” left the ailing patient “in a helpless situation, abandoning him to his fate.”
He accused them of having “breached their duties, performed actions contrary to the art of healing” and having “omitted all the acts they were required to perform.”
The defendants are charged with “dolo eventual” — a legal term meaning that a person is aware that their actions could cause harm but persisted nonetheless.
The highest prison sentence sought by prosecutors was 12 years, for Maradona’s personal physician, Leopoldo Luque.
Other sentences ranging from four to 10 years were sought for other medical staff, which include a psychiatrist, nurse and coordinators.
The health workers have argued that Maradona’s death could not have been foreseen and that they did their jobs. Each defendant has also downplayed their own individual responsibility for his care.
No defibrillator
The case has revolved around whether the doctors’ decision to allow Maradona to convalesce in a private home, instead of in a hospital, was negligent.

The prosecution has also pointed to the near-total absence of medical equipment, such as a hospital bed, defibrillator or quickly available ambulance as evidence of what they presented as the defendants’ dereliction of duty.
Several medical experts testified that Maradona’s carers failed to react to key warning signs — he was suffering from edema, tachycardia and had difficulty breathing — in the lead-up to his death.
“Diego Armando Maradona’s death clearly did not come out of nowhere: the signs of this fatal outcome began to appear long beforehand,” assistant prosecutor Cosme Iribarren summarised yesterday.
The prosecution again showed the court shock images of the former footballer lying dead in bed, his stomach grotesquely swollen.
Maradona’s three daughters, who were present in court yesterday for the start of the summation, covered their faces to avoid seeing the images.
The summation is expected to last around two weeks and the verdict is expected at a later date.

The first trial over Maradona’s death was dramatically annulled last year after two-and-a-half months of hearings, following revelations that one of the judges took part in a clandestine documentary about the case. — AFP
3722e78d371bcecb: ISKANDAR PUTERI, Oct 9 — Johor Darul Ta’zim (JDT) recorded a stylish and commanding victory by crushing PKR Svay Rieng FC 6-0 in Group B of the Asean Club Championship (ACC) 2026/2027 at the Sultan Ibrahim Stadium, here last night.

JDT started fiercely and almost opened the scoring as early as the seventh minute, but striker Jairo da Silva’s attempt after receiving a pass from Oscar Arribas only rattled the crossbar, before winger Arif Aiman Mohd Hanapi’s follow-up shot also went wide.
The visiting Cambodian club’s goalkeeper, Dara Vireak, also successfully tipped away a long-range shot by Molina Martinez in the 36th minute.

The Southern Tigers’ relentless attacks finally paid off when Arif Aiman broke the deadlock in the 39th minute through a powerful shot from outside the penalty box, courtesy of an assist by winger Marcos Guilherme.

Resuming in the second half, JDT further solidified their lead when Marcos Guilherme put his name on the scoresheet as the second goalscorer in the 51st minute after finishing off a pass from Jairo da Silva.
JDT defender Kevin Medina added to the visitors’ misery ten minutes later with an easy header to score the third goal.

The visitors attempted to mount a comeback to narrow the deficit through PKR Svay Rieng FC striker Martins Junior in the 64th minute, but his shot was cleanly saved by JDT goalkeeper Ahmad Syihan Hazmi Mohamed.

Striker Shahab Zahedi further compounded the visitors’ woes by capitalising on a chance inside the penalty box for JDT’s fourth goal in the 70th minute, before Muhammad Daniesh Amiruddin stole the spotlight with two quickfire goals in the 75th and 76th minutes.
The 6-0 scoreline remained until the final whistle. — Bernama
1c3f6579f8e07b13: KUALA LUMPUR: Nineteen cases involving 12 politicians were granted a discharge not amounting to an acquittal (DNAA) in the High Court and lower courts nationwide between 2010 and July this year.

Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Law and Institutional Reform) Datuk Seri Azalina Othman Said said the figures were based on information from the Office of the Chief Registrar of the Federal Court and a review of criminal case records.
She said, unlike civil cases, criminal cases were not subject to a limitation period, meaning individuals granted a DNAA could still be charged again with the same offences.

"This procedure may be undertaken if the prosecution decides to do so, based on the facts, evidence and developments in the case," she said in a written parliamentary reply published on the Parliament website.
She was responding to Pang Hok Liong (PH-Labis), who asked about the number of criminal cases involving politicians and high-profile leaders that had been granted a DNAA.
Azalina said details of specific cases could be obtained directly from the Attorney-General's Chambers, which holds the relevant prosecution records and information.
She clarified that a DNAA did not amount to an acquittal.
cc22bc1047231a03: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 9 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, who is also Finance Minister, will table Budget 2027 in the Dewan Rakyat at 3.30pm today, half an hour earlier than the usual 4pm slot.

The 5th Madani Budget, themed “Malaysia Madani: Menggapai di Langit, Mengakar di Bumi”, is the second Budget under the 13th Malaysia Plan (13MP). The Budget comes at a time when the government seeks to sustain economic momentum while raising the nation’s growth ceiling, improving living standards and strengthening governance.

With the economy on solid ground, the focus leading up to Budget 2027 will be on sustaining this momentum. The economy is projected to grow by 6.0 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, while full-year growth is expected to stay within the government’s forecast range of 4.0 to 5.0 per cent.

Against this backdrop, fiscal policy will remain crucial in supporting economic growth while strengthening fiscal resilience, particularly amid external uncertainties, elevated energy costs and persistent cost pressures.
Efforts to improve public spending efficiency, strengthen revenue mobilisation and reduce leakages are expected to remain part of the government’s fiscal consolidation agenda.

Subsidy rationalisation, one of the key fiscal tools, will remain an important consideration as the government seeks to ensure public resources are channelled more effectively towards targeted assistance and productive economic activities.
The challenge will be to preserve fiscal space while ensuring that subsidy reforms do not undermine household consumption or raise operating costs for businesses.

Development expenditure will continue to be a vital component for supporting economic activity and addressing infrastructure gaps, with spending expected to concentrate on projects that enhance connectivity and productivity.

Water infrastructure, flood mitigation, rural development, utilities and electricity networks, particularly in Sabah and Sarawak and other underserved areas, could remain among the key areas of attention.

On the investment front, Budget 2027 is expected to reinforce Malaysia’s shift towards higher-value economic activities, with greater emphasis on industries capable of generating higher productivity, quality employment and technology transfer.

Continued investment in digitalisation, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing and supporting energy, water and digital infrastructure will be integral to strengthening Malaysia’s competitiveness and position in regional supply chains.

For businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises and micro, small and medium enterprises, measures to improve productivity, facilitate technology adoption and strengthen access to financing will be necessary as they navigate higher operating costs and wage pressures.
A stronger domestic business ecosystem would also help ensure that investment and economic expansion generate wider linkages across the economy.

Ultimately, Budget 2027 will be measured not simply by the size of its allocations, but by how effectively fiscal resources are translated into sustainable growth, productive investment, stronger domestic businesses and quality employment, while keeping public finances on a sustainable path.
The challenge is to ensure that Malaysia’s economic resilience is converted into a stronger foundation for the next phase of growth under the Madani Economy framework. — Bernama
3d5846c25c49004f: MANCHESTER, Oct 9 — Erling Haaland said Manchester City must “stick together” in uncertain times after being found guilty of over 100 charges of breaking Premier League financial rules.

City face a severe points penalty or even expulsion from the Premier League after an independent commission found they used “sham” commercial contracts to inflate revenue and cut costs by over £900 million (RM4.9 billion) between 2009 and 2018.
Haaland did not join City until 2022 but it is the current squad that could bear the burden of any sanction.
Premier League leaders City return to action for the first time since the guilty verdict was revealed at Liverpool on Sunday.
“We have to stay positive, look ahead and try to win football games and try to enjoy the situation and win the game,” Haaland told the club’s website.
“We have to stick together, and we have to spread the love to each other.
“So yeah, stick together, enjoy the ride and smile.”
Haaland signed a contract until 2034 last year, but his future is likely to depend on the severity of any sanction.
The Norwegian has scored 169 goals in 205 games for the club and also shone in spearheading his country’s run to the World Cup quarter-finals.
Europe’s top teams would be lining up for the 26-year-old should City face dropping out of the Premier League or even a prolonged spell without Champions League football.
“I care a lot about City, I have to say,” added Haaland, whose father, Alf-Inge Haaland, also played for the club.
“I care a lot about the fans because I’m a fan myself — I feel with them as well.”
Maresca trusts club ‘completely’
City manager Enzo Maresca echoed Haaland’s call for unity.
“Personally, I’m very calm, to be honest,” Maresca told City’s website.
“The club has been quite clear. We trust completely the club. We understand the noise but the focus for us is just what we can control and we can control just the football side.

“We need to be all together. I said many times the reason why this organisation in the last 15 years was top was because from the owner, the CEO, the sporting director, the manager, players, fans, they are all on the same page. And this is fantastic.”

City have made a perfect start to the Premier League season, winning all of their opening five games, with Maresca insisting the mood among his squad is “fantastic” following a lengthy international break.
“The players are excited for the next two games,” he said.
“But especially they are excited because in this moment we are top of the league. The players are just focused on that.
“They know what we can control is the football side –- they are not worried at all about different things.”

He added: “They know their profession and they know that the noise is there, but they don’t care too much about the noise. They are just focused in this moment on how we can beat Liverpool and how, together with the fans, we can try to win in Anfield.” — AFP
99872eb296730d7a: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 9 — The Federation of Malaysian Manufacturers (FMM) has pressed for decisive, measurable regional action from Asean to eliminate transboundary haze, warning that recurring pollution inflicts severe damage on public health, worker safety, and economic productivity.

The industrial group issued the appeal as severe haze blanketed the country, with Department of Environment (DOE) data recording 38 out of 68 national monitoring stations in the unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) bracket this morning, led by Seremban at 186.
In a statement today, FMM president Jacob Lee Chor Kok stressed that industrial and economic expansion must not come at the expense of environmental sustainability.
“Clean air is not a luxury. It is a fundamental requirement for public health, economic productivity and sustainable development,” the statement said.

The federation said that persistent haze triggers widespread workforce absenteeism, disrupts open-air logistics and factory schedules, and escalates operating overheads through mandatory purchases of protective equipment and industrial air filtration.

While acknowledging existing regional frameworks, including the 2003 Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution and the Asean Haze-Free Roadmap 2023-2030, FMM stressed that member states must shift from diplomatic consensus to rapid, verifiable execution.
To break the annual cycle of smoke pollution, FMM outlined five priority interventions for regional governments:

First, member states must upgrade monitoring and early warning systems by fusing real-time satellite imagery, ground-level API sensors, and meteorological data with artificial intelligence. Rapid alerts are vital to ensure factory operators can execute workplace safety protocols before air quality deteriorates.

Second, Asean must enforce zero-tolerance penalties against illegal open burning at source. Member countries must accelerate peatland rehabilitation under the Second Asean Peatland Management Strategy 2023-2030, while providing smallholders and rural farming communities with affordable, non-burning clearing alternatives.

Third, the federation called for responsible regional supply chains. Large corporations must implement strict environmental due diligence and supply traceability, assist small and medium enterprise (SME) vendors with environmental compliance, and curtail emissions from their own plants during haze episodes.

Fourth, Asean must fast-track financing, clean technology, and scientific research. FMM urged the rapid mobilization of capital under the Asean Investment Framework for Haze-Free Sustainable Land Management, which aims to raise US$1.5 billion by 2030, alongside joint academic and industrial research into land stewardship.

The fifth priority focuses on safeguarding frontline workforces. FMM urged employers to implement the Department of Occupational Safety and Health (DOSH) advisory issued on Oct 6, which cautions that fine particulate matter, including PM2.5, easily penetrates buildings through mechanical ventilation and air-conditioning systems.

Under DOSH guidelines, manufacturers should curtail strenuous outdoor labour when the API breaches 100 and halt it entirely if readings exceed 200. Employers must provide certified respiratory protection where risks cannot be controlled, offer scheduling flexibility to staff affected by school closures, and activate business continuity plans.
Regionally, FMM called on the Asean Secretariat to publish regular public scorecards tracking progress against haze reduction targets, enforcement milestones, and fund mobilization.

Domestically, the federation urged the federal government to leverage Budget 2027 to expand tax allowances and matching grants for industrial green technologies, pollution abatement, and SME investments in workplace air quality monitoring.
“A haze-free Asean must become a measurable achievement, not merely a recurring aspiration,” the statement said.

ef2f88939541ee0e: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 9 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, who is also Finance Minister, is scheduled to table Budget 2027 in the Dewan Rakyat at 3.30pm today.

The tabling will be the fifth budget under his Madani Government, anchored by a clear commitment to ensure high value growth is translated equitably for the people’s wellbeing while strengthening the country’s economic resilience.

The Budget 2027 tabling will be broadcast live on various local television stations and social media platforms, including Bernama TV, which will also air its Budget 2027 Analysis programme at 8.30pm tonight.
According to the pre-budget statement on the Finance Ministry’s website, Budget 2027 is formulated to build on the strong foundation established through previous budgets.

As the second budget under the 13th Malaysia Plan (13MP), it will continue to pursue the three Madani Economy pillars, namely raising the growth ceiling, raising the living standards floor and driving reforms in public administration governance.

The Finance Ministry said Malaysia’s economy remained resilient following bold structural reforms, including fiscal consolidation and targeted subsidy rationalisation, despite global geopolitical uncertainties and disruptions to international supply chains.

For Budget 2027, the ministry outlined 10 key focuses, including narrowing regional disparities, addressing the cost of living through targeted assistance such as the Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) and Budi Madani, strengthening the social safety net for gig workers and preparing for the country’s ageing population by 2030.

Attention will also be given to basic services such as education and healthcare, technology driven public sector transformation through Government Technology (GovTech), workers’ welfare through a dignified wage, empowering local entrepreneurs through the ‘Made by Malaysia’ initiative, and high value investments such as semiconductors and artificial intelligence (AI).

In a post on X yesterday, Anwar expressed hope that Budget 2027 would further strengthen the country’s economic resilience, ease the cost-of-living burden, create more opportunities and ensure the benefits of development are enjoyed more equitably by all segments of society.
According to the calendar on the official Parliament portal, the Supply (Budget) Bill 2027 will be debated at the policy stage for eight days starting next week.
The winding up by the relevant ministries is scheduled from Oct 26 to 29, followed by the committee stage debate from Nov 2 to 26 before the Bill is passed in the Dewan Rakyat. — Bernama
03f45b1c56665185: WASHINGTON, Oct 9 — President Donald Trump yesterday ruled out attacking Iran before the US midterm elections on November 3, saying Washington was holding “productive discussions” with Tehran.
Trump’s post on his Truth Social platform followed a surge in oil prices yesterday driven by media reports suggesting potential new US strikes prior to those elections.

“I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect...we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections,” he wrote.
“We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he added, without providing additional details.

The Atlantic magazine reported on Wednesday that the White House had asked the Pentagon to develop options to strike Iranian targets that could be used before the midterms. The New York Times published a similar report yesterday, saying the plans were being developed despite Trump’s “ambivalence”.

The rise in crude oil prices has also been fueled by persistent tensions in the Strait of Hormuz — a strategic chokepoint for the global oil trade — as well as hostilities between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

In a recent sign of those tensions, an oil tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar reported being struck “by multiple projectiles,” causing an unspecified number of casualties, the UKMTO maritime agency said Wednesday.
Polls suggest that US voters are strongly dissatisfied over rising fuel prices, linked to the conflict launched by the United States and Israel against Iran in February.

The US leader has repeatedly insisted in recent weeks that the United States has effectively won the Iran war, despite ongoing unrest and a recent security threat that forced the withdrawal of American bombers from a base in England.
But Trump’s claims that prices will fall as soon as the Iran war is over have so far fallen on deaf ears with voters.
The midterm elections will shape the final two years of Trump’s presidential term as his Republican Party risks losing its current grip on Congress.
Although Trump is not on the ballot, he is heavily involved in the campaign, holding numerous rallies in an attempt to limit the damage or even turn the political tide.

Trump has warned he faces a possible third impeachment if Democrats retake the House of Representatives, and the White House is preparing for a slew of investigations into corruption and abuse of power.
The US president also yesterday sought to calm a furore over his comments at a rally earlier this week that Iran could “take out” the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego.
Trump, 80, blamed the “fake and artificial news” for misinterpreting the remarks, which Democrats pounced on.

“In actuality, what I was talking about was that a temporary increase in the price of Gasoline is a small price to pay for Iran not having a Nuclear Weapon and, if you want to see a big price, can you imagine what it would be like if they bombed San Diego and/or Los Angeles?” Trump said on Truth Social. — AFP
4f760b89ea7dc2df: GEORGE TOWN: Penang schools will continue operating as usual, but all outdoor activities must be postponed amid the haze, said the state Education Department.
The department said it was monitoring Air Pollutant Index (API) readings around the clock across four stations in Minden, Seberang Jaya, Seberang Prai, and Balik Pulau.
As of 9.55pm, the average API reading had dropped by 4.5 points from 129 to 124.5.
In a Facebook statement, the department said it took the royal decree of His Majesty Sultan Ibrahim, King of Malaysia on safeguarding the health and welfare of students and school personnel.
"For now, schools in Penang will continue to operate as usual based on current API readings. However, all outdoor activities must be postponed," it said.
The department said these measures aligned with the Education Ministry's directive issued yesterday.
It added that educational institutions must act if haze conditions reach or exceed guidelines, including modifying, postponing, or cancelling outdoor activities.
The department urged parents to monitor their children's health and stay updated via official ministry, department, and school channels.
"Close cooperation between schools and parents is essential to safeguarding students' welfare throughout the haze episode," it added.
The King had advised that schools in areas with prolonged API readings between 150 and 180 be closed due to worsening conditions.
Last night, Education Minister Datuk Seri Fadhlina Sidek said schools in four states, including one district in Pahang, as well as Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, would close today due to worsening haze.
8443d6897485a0cc: MADRID: Jose Mourinho's Real Madrid trail leaders Barcelona by six points as La Liga action resumes this weekend, with Spanish football starting the countdown to the Clasico after the extended international break.

It has not been plain sailing for the Portuguese veteran since he returned to the helm of Los Blancos, with defeats at Real Betis and then rivals Atletico Madrid leaving them fourth after seven games.

"Obviously we want to be first, not second, third, fourth, or fifth. And we want more points than we have. Obviously, obviously," said Mourinho before the international break, before blaming officials for his team's struggles.
Madrid visit Barcelona at Camp Nou on Oct 25 in Mourinho's first Clasico since returning to the Spanish capital this summer, following his first stint at the helm between 2010-2013.
Before then come four tough matches for Madrid, hosting Villarreal on Saturday and then Sevilla in La Liga, as well as facing Roma and RB Leipzig in the Champions League.
Barcelona also have a tricky lead-in to the Clasico, with league games against Getafe and Betis mixed with away games in the Champions League at Galatasaray and holders Paris Saint-Germain.
Hansi Flick's side have been unstoppable so far, winning every single match with devastating attacking force, netting 31 goals in their seven league games.
Whether Mourinho is capable of reining in Spain's dominant domestic side will become clear in the testing fortnight ahead.
While Madrid have shown some signs of improvement from last season's poor campaign under Xabi Alonso and then Alvaro Arbeloa, they still have a lot further to go to trouble Flick's Barca machine.
Mourinho has a host of issues to manage in the coming weeks, including the form of Brazilian winger Vinicius Jr.

The coach has defended the Brazilian while admitting he is not at his "killer" best, but starting with the Yellow Submarine's visit to the Santiago Bernabeu, Vinicius must prove he is worthy of a starting spot.
Mourinho hooked the Brazilian in the 2-1 defeat by Atletico and Vinicius subsequently failed to score for his national team in games against Australia and India.
Mbappe issues
There are also concerns around superstar striker Kylian Mbappe.

The French forward has again impressed in front of goal, scoring seven times in La Liga and maintaining the consistency he has shown since joining Madrid. However, he picked up a minor knee injury while on international duty.

Mbappe did not return immediately to Madrid and posted a video of himself riding a bicycle on social media, a few days after Mourinho had said cycling was something he did not want players to do for safety reasons.

Real Madrid fans are often quick to whistle their own players when unhappy, and Mbappe's recent efforts to promote his Ballon d'Or candidacy have drawn criticism from some supporters, particularly amid frustration at the club's failure to win a major trophy in the past two seasons.
Record signing Yan Diomande has yet to bed into the team fully, while the narrow Champions League win over Inter Milan showed Mourinho's side cannot control matches, despite the good result.

The team's run of one clean sheet in eight matches across all competitions also reflects defensive problems, while Mourinho has criticised his team for not capitalising on chances to finish games off and allowing opponents back in.
Mourinho's and Madrid's complaints about refereeing, most recently and explicitly after the derby defeat by Atletico on Sept 20, can only stave off pressure from the club's own fans for so long.
"If they leave us alone, calmly, and let us compete on equal terms, there's still a long way to go," said the veteran Portuguese coach in the aftermath of that loss.
After three weeks licking their wounds and looking at fixes for the problems that have quickly appeared, Mourinho's Madrid can now start walking that road.
d03b439bbf5e88a7: NEW YORK, Oct 9 — Oil prices soared yesterday following reports that the United States could launch fresh attacks on Iran before next month’s midterm elections, risking further supply disruptions.
But the cost surge eased slightly after US President Donald Trump ruled out hitting Iran before the November vote, saying Washington was holding “productive discussions” with Tehran.
Brent North Sea crude, the international benchmark, rallied to as high as US$105.88 (RM433) a barrel before retreating to US$104.28.
The main US contract, West Texas Intermediate, reached as high as US$93.20 per barrel but eventually closed at US$91.49.
The Atlantic magazine reported that the White House had asked the Pentagon to draw up options for hitting sites in Iran ahead of midterms on November 3.

But with Trump’s Republican party standing a chance of losing both houses of Congress, an escalation in the US-Iran conflict could put even more pressure on the president. Already, Americans are battling record-high diesel prices.
Following the surge in energy costs, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform Thursday that “we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections.”
Still, oil markets are reacting not only to nervousness over Trump’s plans but to “increased Iranian attacks on traffic through the Strait of Hormuz,” said Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates.
Another concern is “Hurricane Isaias coming through the Gulf of Mexico and shutting in a significant amount of oil production,” he said.
Pressure on yields
Meanwhile Yemen’s Houthis took aim at Riyadh airport with missiles and warned staff at oil facilities in Saudi Arabia to leave to avoid being targeted as hostilities escalate.
“The renewed rise in oil prices is intensifying inflation concerns and adding to upward pressure on bond yields,” said Forex.com analyst Fawad Razaqzada.

Yields on government bonds have recently touched highs unseen in more than 20 years as investors fear sustained inflation will force central banks to raise interest rates, thus slowing economic growth and hitting equity market valuations.
The surge in oil prices weighed on stock markets, with Wall Street’s main indexes mostly closing lower.
Europe’s main markets finished the day in the red, including London, although higher oil prices benefited energy majors.
Asia’s leading stock markets tracked losses Wednesday on Wall Street, where technology firms pulled back from recent gains.
Shares in Samsung slid as the South Korean titan forecast a huge increase in quarterly profit that nonetheless failed to meet market expectations.

On Wall Street, shares in SpaceX slid 4.2 per cent following a Financial Times report that Elon Musk’s firm is aiming to raise US$40 billion in bank loans and debt to further its purchases of AI chips from Nvidia.
A Financial Times report that OpenAI is bringing in about US$20 billion less in annualized revenue than investors were led to believe also weighed on markets.
“It raises the question about all AI companies,” said Adam Sarhan of 50 Park Investments. “If OpenAI is missing revenue estimates, what does that mean for the other AI companies?” — AFP
