e84aed2041af3df5: A SONG can capture a single moment in time for many musicians. For singer-composer Royston Sta Maria, the track he wrote for the group Freedom, 'Mulanya Di Sini', became something far more enduring.
The composition has travelled across generations, been performed by countless musicians and four decades after it was first penned, continues to find its place in popular culture.
The journey of 'Mulanya Di Sini' began long before it became a familiar favourite.
Roy, now 74, wrote his first song while with the group Discovery, and went on to compose during his years as part of a singing duo with Datuk Francissca Peter.
He contributed two songs to the duo's first album and another two to their second before they went their separate ways in 1984.

Rather than stopping there, he focused increasingly on songwriting for his two solo albums and began entering his compositions into national and regional competitions, including RTM Pesta Lagu, the Golden Kite Song Festival, Write a Song for Kuala Lumpur and the World Peace Song Festival.
Although he achieved some success in those contests, Roy remained unsatisfied.
What he really wanted was to craft a track that would become a major hit — and, more importantly, stand the test of time.
Then came the tune that would eventually become 'Mulanya Di Sini'.
"I had this tune in my head and kept working on it. It took days. Maybe even a few weeks," he tells NST's Groove.
He kept refining the composition, shifting chords and tweaking lines until he was confident he had created something he could truly be proud of.
Once the melody was ready, he approached lyricist Syed Haron and explained his vision, particularly for the chorus.
The result was a song with a catchy refrain that would become one of its hallmarks.
At the time, Roy was playing the piano during happy hour at the PJ Hilton from 4pm to 7pm. When his set ended, another band would take to the stage: Freedom.

Having become friendly with the musicians, he asked whether they would be interested in recording his new composition. They agreed, and the band recorded a demo that was subsequently submitted to EMI.
40 YEARS AND COUNTING

The breakthrough came when the song was chosen to represent Malaysia at the third Asean Song Festival in 1986, where it took second place. Freedom later released the track alongside their debut album in 1987.
Four decades later, the song has featured in 12 commercials, most recently in a Touch 'n Go campaign which the composer considers another milestone for what he jokingly calls his "lucky song".
Its longevity is equally clear online, where musicians and singers regularly post their own renditions.
The track has graced weddings, television broadcasts, university events and busking sessions alike.
Established acts have also covered it, including Rima Melati and Marcell Siahaan, who released a version on Valentine's Day.
"What makes this song so special to me is that after 40 years, it's still widely popular. On YouTube, there are so many videos of people and musicians performing it."
More than the tally of recordings or commercial placements, he treasures the reaction the song continues to stir in live crowds.
"It brings a lot of joy to the audience whenever it's performed, and it's wonderful to see everyone join in."
REFRESHING A TIMELESS LEGACY

That enduring connection inspired his decision to revisit the track for a new generation as part of an upcoming compilation album featuring his compositions — some recorded by himself and others, like 'Mulanya Di Sini', by fellow artistes.
Initially, Roy wanted to give the classic a contemporary arrangement with younger singers to offer it a new lease of life.
But he and his collaborators eventually agreed that nostalgia was integral to the song's identity.
Rather than replacing the vocalists, they chose to retain the original voices of Freedom's Shuib and the late Seha.

"Using modern technology, the original vocals were extracted and woven into a refreshed production. The arrangement was updated, but carefully restrained so listeners would still instantly recognise the song that has accompanied them for decades."
The new version forms part of a larger personal venture: a 12-track album showcasing his original compositions.
"It's a way of documenting my lifetime of work in music and leaving behind a legacy."
The collection will be released on CD and USB, with plans to make it available across digital streaming platforms as well.
Some tracks feature Roy as a solo vocalist, while others showcase guest collaborations.
Fauziah Latiff joins him on the duets 'Tanpa Noktah' and 'Suka Suka', while another duet features Veronica Nonis.
Freedom performs on 'Mulanya Di Sini' and 'Babak Cinta Terakhir', with various guest artistes performing the remaining tracks.

The album is not simply a reissue of old recordings; it is a snapshot of a musical life shaped by bands, songwriting, competitions, live gigs and collaborations, alongside a steady resolve to keep creating as the industry transforms around him.
KEEPING LIVE MUSIC ALIVE
For Roy, that transformation is especially noticeable in the live music scene.
"Back then, there were always bands playing in hotels. You'd hear live music in the lobby, or even in coffeehouses. Nowadays, the piano often sits in a corner purely as decoration."
Today, he observes, live bands are mostly restricted to pubs, with many venues opting for smaller two- or three-piece set-ups
This shifting landscape has made it increasingly challenging for musicians, especially veterans, to earn a steady living.
It's why he considers Musicians for Malaysia (MfM) benefit concert on Oct 10 so vital. He is set to travel from Perth to join the line-up.
Beyond celebrating veteran talent, the event aims to raise funds and create fresh opportunities for performers impacted by the decline of traditional live music venues.
"Continuing to perform is about more than nostalgia. It's about keeping live music alive — and ensuring that the musicians who spent decades entertaining audiences aren't forgotten."
Roy recently performed at Pesta San Pedro in Melaka and will next take the stage at the MfM concert.
Meanwhile, 'Mulanya Di Sini' continues its journey, finding its way into new commercials, fresh performances and another generation's playlists.

3586888a689fb75d: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 9 — Air quality remained at unhealthy levels across broad swathes of Malaysia this morning, prompting the closure of all schools in Selangor, Melaka, and Negeri Sembilan as Seremban logged the nation’s highest Air Pollutant Index (API) reading at 186.
According to Department of Environment (DOE) surveillance data as of 8.30am, 38 out of 68 monitoring stations nationwide recorded unhealthy air quality (API 101 to 200).
None of the stations recorded good air quality, 30 registered moderate levels, and none breached the very unhealthy benchmark of 201.

Seven monitoring stations exceeded the critical 180 mark this morning. Following Seremban (186), the next highest readings were recorded in Bandaraya Melaka at 184, alongside a three-way tie at 183 among Nilai in Negeri Sembilan, Bukit Rambai in Melaka, and Segamat in Johor. Peat fire flashpoint Johan Setia in Selangor recorded 182, while Tangkak in Johor stood at 181.
Just below the 180 threshold, elevated figures were logged in Pasir Gudang (179), Shah Alam (178), and Alor Gajah (177).
In Perak, Tasek Ipoh posted 176, Tanjung Malim 173, and Pegoh Ipoh 171. Kluang in Johor also registered 176, while Port Dickson logged 174.
Across the Greater Klang Valley, Batu Muda in Kuala Lumpur recorded 172, with Cheras and Putrajaya both tied at 170. Petaling Jaya and Banting each recorded 169, while Klang posted 168.
In Johor, Larkin recorded 172, Batu Pahat and Pengerang stood at 169 each, and Kota Tinggi logged 164. On the East Coast, Rompin in Pahang stood at 170.

Readings were comparatively lower in the north and east, though still within the unhealthy band. These included Indera Mahkota Kuantan (162), Seri Manjung (159), Sungai Petani (157), Temerloh (154), Minden and Kemaman (153 each), Alor Setar (152), Seberang Jaya (151), Kuala Selangor (145), Taiping (130), Seberang Perai (120), and Balok Baru Kuantan, which posted the lowest unhealthy reading at 107.
All primary and secondary schools across Selangor, Melaka, and Negeri Sembilan are closed today following directives from the Ministry of Education.

Under ministry guidelines announced yesterday, all educational institutions in areas where API readings breach 180 must suspend physical classes and transition immediately to home-based teaching and learning (PdPR).
The ministry also instructed that schools in districts where API levels linger above 150 for three consecutive days must close from Monday, October 12.

Education Director-General Datuk Mohd Azam Ahmad said the pre-emptive closures were implemented to shield students and educators from hazardous particulate exposure, following royal concerns expressed by His Majesty Sultan Ibrahim, the King of Malaysia.
The DOE attributed the choking haze to prolonged dry weather and hundreds of fire hotspots across Sumatra and Kalimantan.

Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim yesterday described the situation as alarming, confirming that the government has intensified cloud seeding operations in cloud-viable zones to mitigate the pollution.
68a1606a35055f25: LONDON, Oct 9 — Disgraced former prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor won a legal challenge over searches of his royal homes after police agreed the warrants they obtained were “unlawful”, a High Court judge disclosed yesterday.
However, the London court must still decide whether police can continue to hold items seized in the raids, with both the judge and police stressing the investigation remained ongoing.
King Charles III’s brother was arrested on his 66th birthday in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office related to links to late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
He was released the same day, after hours of police questioning, but has remained under investigation. He has denied all wrongdoing in connection with the American financier.

Thames Valley Police (TVP) searched his former home in Windsor, west of London, and Sandringham, eastern England, but it has now emerged Andrew launched a legal challenge over the legality of the warrants used.

In reporting the challenge, the Daily Telegraph noted that it was the first time a member of Britain’s royal family has challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of Charles I in 1649.
‘Warrants quashed’
In the first detailed public disclosures about Andrew’s action, judge Nicholas Hilliard yesterday revealed the police had agreed “the search warrants were unlawful”.

But “the fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring an investigation to an end, or mean that the whole of the investigation was unlawful. TVP are continuing with their investigations,” he added.

Hilliard said he would decide “in due course” on a June legal application by police to retain property obtained under an unlawful warrant “if it would be lawful to seize the property” under a new warrant.
“There would be little point in handing property back if it could then simply be lawfully seized under some other provision,” he explained of the police request.
His 10-page order noted that Andrew “opposes the application” to keep the seized items, with a private court hearing on the matter to be held next year.
In a statement, the police said they accepted “the initial court’s decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.”
‘Ongoing’ probe
But it added “legal proceedings are currently ongoing to decide how material seized during the searches will be managed and whether we can lawfully retain it in support of our ongoing investigation”.
“We continue to pursue all reasonable lines of enquiry to effectively and fairly progress this investigation,” the force said.
Royal commentator and historian Andrew Lownie told AFP the ruling was “psychologically... a boost for Andrew’s campaign”.
“He is quite bombastic, he does feel he’s been wronged. And he now feels that he should be fighting back rather than just taking all the punches,” said Lownie.
Andrew’s arrest and the police searches marked a new low for the ex-prince, who was stripped of his royal titles last year and ousted from his Windsor home over his Epstein connections.
The government has even mulled passing a law to remove him from the line of succession.

Scandal has engulfed the king’s younger brother since one of Epstein’s accusers, Virginia Giuffre, claimed in her posthumous memoirs that she had been trafficked three times to have sex with Andrew when she was a teenager.
The former prince has repeatedly denied the claims. He settled a US civil lawsuit in 2022 brought by Giuffre while not admitting liability.

The police probe follows new revelations from documents relating to the American financier released by the United States this year, including emails in which Andrew appeared to share potentially confidential information with him. — AFP
6ce1e227b7aec959: LUCERNE, (Switzerland): Switzerland national football team and Sunderland captain Granit Xhaka said Thursday that he received a suspended fine of 150,000 Swiss francs (US$180,000) after admitting to obtaining a fake Covid-19 vaccination certificate during the pandemic, Anadolu Ajansi reported.

The Swiss Football Association said it would hold additional discussions with Xhaka following the conclusion of legal proceedings. — BERNAMA

74ce9e1e74983f06: KUALA LUMPUR: A monthly salary of about RM3,100 for a single person in Kuala Lumpur should be seen as a financial baseline for a reasonable standard of living, not a guarantee of financial comfort.

Universiti Putra Malaysia (UPM) Faculty of Human Ecology dean and personal financial planning lecturer Prof Dr Mohamad Fazli Sabri said the figure could serve as a benchmark for assessing whether a person could meet basic needs while setting aside some savings and preparing for emergencies.

Fazli said income adequacy should not be measured solely by one's ability to pay for food, rent and transport, but should also account for healthcare, communication, social participation, savings and protection against financial shocks.
"Minimum wage is the lowest wage set through policy and legislation. A living wage addresses a broader question: after working full-time, does a person earn enough to live reasonably?
"This includes having some savings and financial protection, rather than merely having enough to get by until the end of the month," he told Berita Harian.
It was previously reported that a single person living in Kuala Lumpur was estimated to need a living wage of about RM3,100 a month to maintain a reasonable standard of living.
The estimate was based on the 2026 Government-Linked Enterprises Activation and Reform Programme (GEAR-uP) initiative, which accounted for changes in the cost of living.
Fazli said RM3,100 was a reasonable starting point, but it was too early to consider it a comfortable salary, as financial well-being depended largely on individual commitments and spending habits.

"Someone who rents a room near their workplace and uses public transport would have a different financial position from someone who owns a car, pays a loan, rents a place alone and supports their parents," he said.
He said it was therefore wrong to assume that every single person earning RM3,100 automatically enjoyed financial well-being.
Differences in transport costs also illustrated how lifestyle choices could affect income adequacy, particularly in urban areas.

Citing the Belanjawanku 2024/2025 guide, he said estimated monthly expenses for a single person in the Klang Valley stood at about RM1,970 for public transport users, compared with RM2,800 for car owners.
"This difference shows that transport choices alone can have a significant impact on a person's financial position," he said.

Fazli said the financial margin would shrink further for those with commitments such as National Higher Education Fund Corporation (PTPTN) loans, insurance or takaful payments, parental support and emergency savings.

"For example, someone earning RM3,100 may be able to pay all their bills, but if only RM50 or RM100 remains after meeting all their commitments, a minor emergency, such as a car breakdown or illness, could force them to use a credit card, buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) services or borrow from family," he said.

aff3234397923ac1: KUALA LUMPUR: The race is long over, but Malaysian fans are still reliving Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia through "cinematic video clips" of cars speeding past Sepang's grandstands against an orange sunset.
Videos circulating on Threads capture the evening atmosphere at Sepang International Circuit, with the fading sunlight and haze lending the event a movie-like quality.
One video posted by user @mxrul drew more than 42,500 likes and 311,000 views.
"Like something out of a movie. Only the haze spoils it," the user wrote.

User @saifuddinsuhaimy, whose video drew 638,000 views and 68,500 likes, wrote: "This is the most beautiful and priceless scene in F1, with the sunset as a backdrop. Hopefully, we'll meet again at Sepang."
Amid fans sharing their memories, some also called for a permanent return of F1 to Sepang.
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the Oct 4 race, ahead of Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and Ferrari's Hamilton.
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim had said the government is discussing Malaysia's return to the F1 calendar.
The Oct 2 to 4 event marked F1's return to the circuit after a nine-year absence, with Sepang last hosting a race in 2017.
The Bahrain GP was relocated to Sepang following an agreement involving the Malaysian and Bahrain governments, F1 and the FIA.

d0240b4589afc2d9: KUALA LUMPUR: Ahli Parlimen Klang V Ganabatirau memfailkan saman fitnah terhadap penceramah Firdaus Wong di Mahkamah Tinggi berhubung hantaran media sosial didakwa mempersoalkan kesetiaannya kepada Malaysia.
Ganabatirau berkata, hantaran diterbitkan di akaun Facebook dan Instagram Firdaus pada 28 Julai itu berunsur fitnah dan mencemarkan reputasi, integriti serta kewibawaannya sebagai wakil rakyat.
Hantaran tersebut dibuat susulan pertemuan Ganabatirau dengan Narendra Modi sempena lawatan perdana menteri India itu ke Malaysia, pada 8 Feb.

Menurut pernyataan tuntutan, Ganabatirau membangkitkan kebimbangan dengan Modi mengenai syarat-syarat kemudahan kad warganegara luar negara India (OCI) dan memohon kelonggaran lebih besar bagi rakyat Malaysia berketurunan India yang layak.
Ganabatirau berkata, Firdaus mempersoalkan motifnya yang 'bersungguh-sungguh' meminta kelonggaran berkenaan pada pertemuan tersebut.
Hantaran itu turut menggambarkan OCI sebagai 'kad warganegara India luar negara' dan diakhiri dengan ungkapan 'Ganabatirau setia kepada Malaysia', berserta emoji memberi tabik hormat.
Ganabatirau mendakwa, kenyataan penutup itu berunsur sarkastik dan bukannya pengesahan terhadap kesetiaannya, serta bertujuan memberi bayangan bahawa kesetiaannya kepada Malaysia diragui.

Beliau berkata, hantaran berkenaan apabila dibaca secara keseluruhan, memberi tanggapan kesetiaannya berbelah bahagi antara Malaysia dan India, dan bahawa beliau mengutamakan kepentingan India berbanding Malaysia.

Ahli Parlimen itu turut menegaskan, kemudahan OCI tidak menganugerahkan kewarganegaraan India, sambil menambah tiada apa-apa dalam kenyataan asalnya yang membayangkan rakyat Malaysia perlu melepaskan kewarganegaraan atau kesetiaan mereka kepada Malaysia.
Saman itu menyatakan akaun Facebook Firdaus mempunyai sekitar 140,000 pengikut, manakala akaun Instagram mempunyai sekitar 387,000 pengikut.
Hantaran Facebook terbabit menerima sekitar 963 reaksi, 207 komen dan 139 perkongsian, manakala hantaran Instagram meraih sekitar 1,525 tanda suka dan 163 komen.
Ganabatirau berkata, beliau mengeluarkan surat tuntutan pada 4 Ogos untuk meminta penarikan balik hantaran, permohonan maaf serta pemadaman hantaran itu.
Beliau mendakwa, Firdaus enggan mematuhinya selain mempertahankan tohmahan berkenaan secara terbuka.
Ganabatirau menuntut ganti rugi am, ganti rugi teruk, dan ganti rugi teladan, perintah injunksi bagi menghalang penerbitan berlanjutan, pemadaman hantaran, serta permohonan maaf terbuka.
Saman itu difailkan semalam menerusi firma guaman Tetuan SN Nair & Partners.
f7b61e38e5a6e845: PETALING JAYA: An electoral understanding between Pakatan Harapan (PH) and Bersatu in the Melaka polls will not stand a chance if Umno and PAS agree on an alliance, an analyst said.

James Chin of the University of Tasmania said both PH and Bersatu appeared desperate for a pact with each other, even an informal one, especially after the Barisan Nasional-Perikatan Nasional alliance’s convincing win in the Negeri Sembilan polls.

“Both are pushed into a corner, and they think the best way to approach Umno-PAS is for a pact to be formed between them. But if Umno and PAS can reach a deal, then the PH-Bersatu pact will fail, except in DAP areas,” he told FMT.

Chin said the main justification for a PH-Bersatu alliance — despite their history of bitter enmity — was to ensure straight fights to prevent the splitting of votes by electors who were against Umno and PAS.

Bersatu, co-founded by former prime minister Muhyiddin Yassin, is a former PH component that played a key role in the collapse of the PH-led federal government in February 2020, resulting in Muhyiddin taking over as prime minister.
Despite being a co-founder of PN, Bersatu has fallen out of favour in the coalition after falling out with PAS, which currently chairs the opposition entity.
In the Aug 1 Negeri Sembilan polls, the BN-PN pact secured a two-thirds majority with 25 seats while PH won the remaining 11. Bersatu contested 24 seats but lost heavily in all.
In the 2021 Melaka polls, BN won 21 seats while PH took five and PN two as the three coalitions clashed in all 28 seats.

Universiti Sains Malaysia’s Ahmad Fauzi Abdul Hamid argued that Bersatu could provide PH with a crucial boost in votes, especially since 10 of the 21 seats BN secured in 2021 were won with marginal majorities.

They are Serkam (79-vote majority), Pengkalan Batu (131), Duyong (200), Tanjung Bidara (364), Gadek (559), Durian Tunggal (559), Paya Rumput (629), Pantai Kundor (827), Rembia (860), and Kelebang (876).
He said Bersatu could help deliver just enough Malay-Muslim votes to help PH pip its opponents to win these marginal seats.
“BN’s dominance in Melaka is not as overwhelming as it seems. With the help of a few thousand more Malay-Muslim votes, it might just be enough for PH to tip the scales in Melaka,” said Fauzi.
“With Bersatu as PH’s partner, it gives some assurance to Malay-Muslim voters that their plight would not be overlooked should the PH-Bersatu alliance come to power in Melaka, and even nationally.”
Nonetheless, he said Bersatu would be more desperate for a pact with PH than the other way around, as Muhyiddin’s party would want to avoid a repeat of its heavy defeats in the Negeri Sembilan polls.

“For PH, while a tie-up with Bersatu may offer some benefits, Bersatu is not indispensable. PH can do without Bersatu, but for Bersatu, going it alone in Melaka would only be a repetition of the Negeri Sembilan polls.”
Voters in Melaka go to the polls for the 16th state election on Nov 14.
3c2c5aedae91e7f3: PETALING JAYA: Kerjasama Pakatan Harapan (PH) dan Bersatu pada PRN Melaka dijangka sukar menandingi gabungan Umno dan PAS sekiranya kedua-dua parti itu mencapai kesepakatan, menurut penganalisis.

James Chin dari Universiti Tasmania berkata PH dan Bersatu dilihat semakin terdesak untuk bekerjasama, walaupun secara tidak rasmi, terutama selepas kemenangan besar gabungan Barisan Nasional (BN) dan Perikatan Nasional (PN) pada PRN Negeri Sembilan, Ogos lalu.

"Kedua-duanya kini tersepit dan melihat kerjasama sebagai jalan terbaik untuk berdepan Umno-PAS. Namun, jika Umno dan PAS mencapai persetujuan, kerjasama PH-Bersatu akan gagal, kecuali di kawasan DAP," katanya kepada FMT.

Chin berkata kerjasama PH-Bersatu, walaupun kedua-duanya mempunyai sejarah permusuhan politik, bertujuan memastikan pertandingan satu lawan satu bagi mengelakkan perpecahan undi dalam kalangan pengundi yang menentang Umno dan PAS.
Bersatu yang diasaskan bersama Muhyiddin Yassin pernah bekerjasama dengan PH, sebelum memainkan peranan penting dalam kejatuhan kerajaan persekutuan pimpinan gabungan itu pada Februari 2020.
Keadaan itu membawa Muhyiddin mengambil alih jawatan perdana menteri.
Walaupun antara pengasas PN, kedudukan Bersatu dalam gabungan itu semakin terpinggir susulan perselisihan dengan PAS yang kini menerajui gabungan pembangkang berkenaan.
Pada PRN Negeri Sembilan, 1 Ogos lalu, kerjasama BN-PN berjaya memperoleh majoriti dua pertiga dengan memenangi 25 kerusi, manakala PH meraih baki 11 kerusi.
Bersatu pula mengalami kekalahan besar di semua 24 kerusi yang ditandinginya.
Pada PRN Melaka 2021, BN memenangi 21 kerusi, PH lima dan PN dua, dalam pertandingan yang menyaksikan ketiga-tiga gabungan bertembung di semua 28 kerusi DUN.
Penting tetapi bukan penentu

Ahmad Fauzi Abdul Hamid dari Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM) pula berpandangan Bersatu mampu membantu PH meraih undi tambahan, terutama di 10 daripada 21 kerusi yang dimenangi BN pada 2021 dengan majoriti tipis.
Kerusi berkenaan ialah Serkam (majoriti 79 undi), Pengkalan Batu (131), Duyong (200),
Tanjung Bidara (364), Gadek (559), Durian Tunggal (559), Paya Rumput (629), Pantai Kundor (827), Rembia (860) dan Kelebang (876).
Fauzi berkata Bersatu berpotensi menyumbang undi Melayu-Islam yang diperlukan PH untuk mengatasi lawan di kerusi marginal berkenaan.
"Penguasaan BN di Melaka sebenarnya tidaklah sekuat yang disangka. Dengan tambahan beberapa ribu undi Melayu-Islam, PH mungkin mampu mengubah keputusan pilihan raya di negeri itu," katanya.

Menurutnya, kerjasama dengan Bersatu juga boleh memberi keyakinan kepada pengundi Melayu-Islam bahawa kepentingan mereka tidak akan diabaikan sekiranya gabungan PH-Bersatu membentuk kerajaan di Melaka, malah pada peringkat persekutuan.

Bagaimanapun, Fauzi berkata Bersatu lebih memerlukan kerjasama dengan PH berbanding sebaliknya kerana parti pimpinan Muhyiddin itu mahu mengelakkan kekalahan besar seperti yang dialaminya pada PRN Negeri Sembilan.

"Bagi PH, kerjasama dengan Bersatu mungkin membawa manfaat, tetapi parti itu bukanlah rakan yang wajib ada. PH masih boleh bergerak tanpa Bersatu, tetapi jika Bersatu bertanding sendirian di Melaka, keputusan PRN Negeri Sembilan mungkin berulang," katanya.
PRN Melaka akan berlangsung 14 Nov depan.
ade6df244998e558: DENGKIL: When was the last time you heard birds chirping, felt a cool breeze brushing against your face and enjoyed a kampung-style breakfast early in the morning?
At Warung E’Jeap in Dengkil, mornings feel a world away from the rush of the city.

Tucked along a small lane away from the main road, the warung sits amid trees, older houses and plenty of greenery. There is little to suggest that you are anywhere near the bustle of modern life, which perhaps explains why it is famous among the local residents.

Warung E’Jeap has been around since 1996, and its menu appears to have stayed true to that uncomplicated spirit. There is no lengthy list of dishes to choose from - just a handful of familiar local breakfast favourites such as roti canai, nasi lemak, lontong and soto.
The tables and chairs are simple and somewhat makeshift, while the overall setting is decidedly that of an old-school kampung eatery.
Warung E’Jeap opens at 6.30am, and some of its more popular dishes, particularly the lontong, can sell out fairly quickly. So if you have your heart set on trying it, get there early.

Once you try the lontong, you’ll understand why people are willing to make the trip here. Served in a spicy coconuty vegetable broth, it has enough heat to jolt the senses awake first thing in the morning. The broth is packed with flavour, while the various condiments - such as the fried tempeh, hard-boiled egg, and of course the nasi impit - add different textures and tastes to each mouthful.

The roti telur goyang is another equally satisfying dish worth trying. Two soft-boiled eggs are expertly placed atop the roti which itself is flaky, buttery and fresh from the griddle. A little kicap and spicy sambal added to the mix brings another welcome hit of heat.
One thing to keep in mind, however, is that early birds really do get the food here. And if the food is what brings you here, the setting is what makes you want to stay.

There is something particularly relaxing about sitting down to breakfast without the constant hum of traffic in the background. Instead, you hear birds chirping, see random chickens casually walking past, and feel the cool morning air around you.
That atmosphere also makes Warung E’Jeap feel different from the typical roadside breakfast stop. It is not polished or trendy, nor is it trying to be. Its appeal lies precisely in its simplicity.

Ultimately, for those looking for an uncomplicated Malaysian breakfast in a peaceful kampung setting, Warung E’Jeap offers a chance to slow down, breathe in some fresh morning air and start the day with good food.
Warung E’Jeap Jalan P5, Kampung Tok Aminuddin 43800 Dengkil, Wilayah Persekutuan Putrajaya

3c34dc8f6a458f65: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 9 — All education institutions under the Education Ministry (MOE) in the Federal Territory of Putrajaya and Selangor have been instructed to close today due to the haze.

The Putrajaya Education Department said the decision is in line with the MOE’s instructions and His Majesty, Sultan Ibrahim, King of Malaysia’s decree out of concerns for the safety and health of students.
The closure is based on the Air Pollution Index (API) readings recorded at monitoring stations as of 5pm yesterday, it added.

Meanwhile, in SHAH ALAM, Selangor state education director Datin Wan Nor Ashikin Abu Kassim confirmed the closure of all MOE education institutions in the state tomorrow, while Selangor Islamic Religious Department director Datuk Mohd Shahzihan Ahmad announced in a separate statement also announced that all state religious schools under the department would be fully closed tomorrow, and recommended that private religious schools registered with the department to follow suit.
In PAHANG, the state education department issued a statement tonight instructing education institutions under its purview in Rompin district to close tomorrow.

“All education institutions in Rompin need to monitor API reading developments continuously and to comply with guidelines and instructions issued by the MOE, the Environmental Department and the Health Ministry,” the department said.

Due to the closure, all education institutions affected need to conduct learning at home to ensure the continuity of learning for students taking into consideration students’ capability, access and needs and teacher readiness.

Upon the consideration of the Education Minister, teachers and implementor group members are also allowed to work from home throughout the closure, while parents are advised to refer to information from official sources.

As of 3pm yesterday, 38 areas in Peninsular Malaysia recorded unhealthy API readings with Segamat, Johor, with the highest reading at 190, followed by Seremban (186) and Nilai (185) in Negeri Sembilan, Kluang in Johor (181), Rompin, Pahang and Johan Setia, Selangor both with readings of 178. — Bernama
086a695ccd3287e8: WASHINGTON, Oct 9 — The execution by firing squad of convicted military base shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed, a Pentagon official said yesterday, after Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said it would be carried out in “public.”

Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist, shot dead 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009. His execution will be the first by the US military since 1961, and the first it has carried out by firing squad since World War II.
“It will be livestreamed. Details will follow,” the Pentagon official told AFP on condition of anonymity.

Hegseth had said in a video posted on X by official Pentagon accounts earlier yesterday that Hasan is “going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public.”
“People need to understand that...there’s serious consequence for these types of things,” Hegseth told right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec while aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier.
Hegseth noted that it would be the military’s first firing squad execution since the Second World War — a reference to the case of Eddie Slovik, who was put to death for desertion in 1945.
“I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win, which was understand when the enemy attacks you, you need to stand your ground,” Hegseth said.
In a separate clip, Posobiec asked the Pentagon chief if Hasan had made any final request.
“Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3,” Hegseth said — the day Hasan is slated to die.
The last US military execution was carried out in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder.
Afghanistan and Iran
According to rights group Amnesty International, at least 17 public executions are known to have been carried out in 2025 — six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran.
The Death Penalty Information Centre says that 135 soldiers have been executed by the US military since 1916.
The Pentagon announced earlier this week that US President Donald Trump had approved Hasan’s execution for carrying out the Al-Qaeda inspired attack.
Twelve of those he killed and 30 of the wounded were soldiers. Hasan was shot and partially paralysed by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack.
He was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013.

Hasan chose to conduct his own defence during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges. Court-appointed defense attorneys expressed concern that he was seeking execution.

The court that convicted Hasan was told he was opposed to the US military’s occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he had spoken online with an alleged Al-Qaeda figure, radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, an American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.
While mass shootings in the United States are common, they are relatively rare at military facilities.
In 2025, a soldier opened fire at a US military base in the state of Georgia, wounding five fellow troops before he was tackled and apprehended.
In 2019, a US sailor fatally shot two people and wounded a third at a base in Hawaii, while a Saudi military student shot dead three people at a military facility in Florida the same year.

And a Kuwaiti-born US citizen attacked two military installations in Tennessee in 2015, killing four Marines and a sailor. The FBI concluded the violence was inspired by a “foreign terrorist group.” — AFP
58db0296bb583a8e: KUALA LUMPUR: Fake International Driving Permits (IDPs) sold to foreigners for up to RM500 have come under scrutiny after authorities uncovered documents linked to websites designed to make them appear legitimate.
The questionable permits, purportedly valid for up to five years, were detected and seized during enforcement operations targeting foreign motorists in the capital.
Checks on one document revealed a website where its serial number could be verified, creating the impression of an official verification system.
The website is believed to have been set up by the syndicate behind the fake permits to mislead motorists and enforcement personnel.

Kuala Lumpur Road Transport Department (RTD) director Hamidi Adam said the department had detected parties offering documents purported to be IDPs to foreigners despite doubts over their validity under Malaysian law.
"We have detected parties offering documents claimed to be International Driving Permits to foreigners for fees of up to RM500, with purported validity periods of up to five years.
"These documents do not meet the recognition requirements for legal driving in Malaysia," he said in a statement.
Hamidi said foreigners who purchased the documents could mistakenly believe they were legally entitled to drive in Malaysia.
He stressed that merely possessing a document bearing the words "International Driving Permit" did not automatically entitle its holder to drive on Malaysian roads.
"Such documents must be issued by the relevant authorities or parties authorised by the country concerned and must fulfil the recognition requirements applicable in Malaysia," he said.
Hamidi pointed out that IDPs issued by Malaysia's RTD were valid for only one year under the Convention on Road Traffic signed in Geneva on Sept 19, 1949.
He said the use of such permits was also subject to the laws and regulations of the respective countries or territories.

The discovery of the questionable documents and their accompanying verification website has highlighted concerns over how easily foreign motorists and enforcement personnel could be misled by documents designed to resemble legitimate international driving credentials.

Although a serial number may appear on a website, this does not necessarily mean the document is recognised by the Malaysian authorities or that its holder is legally permitted to drive in the country.
Hamidi urged foreigners not to be deceived by individuals or organisations offering international driving documents without proper authority or recognition.
"The RTD will not compromise on the use of invalid driving documents. Appropriate enforcement action will be taken against anyone found violating the law," he said.
The discovery comes as Kuala Lumpur RTD intensifies enforcement against foreign motorists through its Ops Pewa.
During yesterday's operation, officers seized 47 of the 121 vehicles inspected, comprising 40 motorcycles, four cars and three goods vehicles.
A total of 273 notices were issued under the Road Transport Act 1987 for offences including driving licence violations, expired motor vehicle licences, insurance breaches and technical infringements.
The operation also saw 58 foreigners, including drivers, pillion riders and vehicle attendants, referred to the Immigration Department for further action.

2558a24dcf3c9217: BOSTON/LONDON/SYDNEY: Global shares slid on Thursday as a mild pullback in sovereign bond yields was countered by a jump in oil prices and indicators of the massive debt that technology companies may need to sustain their dramatic artificial intelligence-fueled growth.

Wall Street's main indexes fell, with the S&P 500 down about 0.5 per cent and the Nasdaq off nearly 1.3 per cent. Chipmakers, which have soared over 80 per cent so far this year, were clear underperformers on the day following a report that OpenAI's annualized revenues were US$20 billion less than the company previously signaled.

Euro zone borrowing costs rose on Thursday as the surge in oil prices intensified inflation concerns, though investors took a breather from selling bonds of heavily indebted countries such as France and Italy. The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes , also pulled back from its elevated levels, dipping 5 basis points to 5.227 per cent. Yields started moving lower after a 30-year bond auction met with solid demand, showing investors remain willing to buy long-dated government debt, despite the ongoing market selloff.
"Markets are going to be watchful if that contagion continues," said Kiran Ganesh, a multi-asset strategist at UBS Global Wealth Management.
"At this stage, the markets would be most comforted by monetary intervention," he added, referring to the ECB buying bonds to ease the market strains.
The pan-European STOXX 600 fell 0.75 per cent to around its lowest since June, while France's CAC-40 dropped 0.5 per cent, nearing its lows for the year in March.
Overnight in Asia, Japan's Nikkei had shed 1.4 per cent and South Korea's chipmaker-heavy KOSPI slumped 2.6 per cent.
AI DEBT RUSH

In commodity markets, oil prices settled 4 per cent higher, with Brent crude futures at US$104.28, on revived concerns about the war in the Middle East and growing supply disruptions due to a hurricane approaching the US Gulf Coast.
The US quarterly earnings season picks up pace next week with big banks, including JPMorgan, set to report results.

Optimism around strong earnings has buoyed US stocks lately despite shaky geopolitical developments and concerns about rising interest rates. The tech and energy sectors are expected to report the biggest quarterly earnings growth, while the broader S&P 500 is expected to post a punchy 30.6 per cent increase in quarterly earnings, according to LSEG data.

Vlad Barbalat, Liberty Mutual Group's chief investment officer and president of global risk & capital solutions, said the S&P 500's roughly 15 per cent return this year looks ordinary on the surface, but the composition is striking.

"The index has risen even as its forward P/E has fallen from roughly 22x to 19x, supported by exceptionally strong growth in rolling forward earnings, all while more than a third of S&P 500 stocks are down," Barbalat wrote in an email. "The result is a historically uncommon combination: a narrow rally in which the market has gotten cheaper even as the index hovers near all-time highs."

Debt remains a strong underwater current. The Wall Street Journal added to media reports on Wednesday that SpaceX , Broadcom and Oracle were all looking to raise serious money to buy high-end AI chips.

Broadcom was looking for US$50 billion in financing, while SpaceX was planning to issue US$30 billion in investment-grade debt and raise US$10 billion in loans to buy chips from Nvidia , which is a major shareholder in SpaceX. SOVEREIGN BONDS VS CORPORATE DEBT

709475b6d759d23c: PETALING JAYA: Anyone who lives with a dog or cat has probably wondered what exactly that bark, whine or indignant meow is supposed to mean. One bark may signal someone at the gate, another excitement, while a particular mewl might appear reliably five minutes before dinner.

Artificial intelligence is now being used to examine those sounds on a much larger scale, analysing thousands of vocalisations and identifying patterns that would be difficult for the human ear to detect.

Researchers at Kaunas University of Technology in Lithuania say AI can already group recurring animal sounds and link them with behaviour or environmental context. Turning that into a genuine animal-to-human translator, however, is far more ambitious.

Machine-learning systems are particularly useful when researchers have huge quantities of audio to examine, comparing features such as pitch, duration, rhythm and frequency to identify recurring patterns.

Research published this year in Frontiers in Veterinary Science, for example, trained a deep-learning system on thousands of dog and cat vocalisations and reported high accuracy when classifying certain emotional states.
That may sound tantalisingly close to translation, but there is an important distinction: recognising a pattern is not the same as understanding meaning.
A bark is not necessarily a word

A computer might learn that one type of bark frequently occurs during play, another when a stranger approaches, and a third during distress. What it cannot automatically tell us is whether the animal is conveying a specific “message” comparable to a human sentence.
Separate research has highlighted this difficulty by testing AI on toddler vocalisations, where humans already have some idea what the sounds are intended to communicate.

Even advanced neural networks sometimes grouped sounds with different meanings together, while separating others that conveyed similar things. The researchers concluded that sound alone is not enough; context and the listener’s response also matter.

With animals, that challenge is greater still. A bark accompanied by a stiff body, raised hackles and a stranger at the gate may mean something very different from a similar-sounding bark produced while chasing a favourite toy.

That is why researchers increasingly look beyond sound to facial expressions, posture, gaze, tail movement, activity and surroundings. Studies involving dogs using communication buttons have likewise cautioned against interpreting an isolated signal without considering what happened before and after it.

The eventual “translator” may therefore look less like a device that turns "woof!" into “I would like chicken, please”, and more like a system combining sound, movement and context to estimate an animal’s emotional state or likely intention.

Such technology could still be useful: AI-assisted systems might help owners recognise stress, fear or discomfort earlier, while vets and animal carers could use vocal patterns as another clue when monitoring wellbeing.
Dr Dolittle will have to wait

Scientists nevertheless urge caution over claims that AI will soon allow humans to “talk” to animals. Researchers quoted recently by The Guardian warned that excitement around animal-language AI can easily outrun the evidence, particularly when commercial products promise more than science has demonstrated.

At present, there is no validated system capable of translating a dog’s thoughts into human language, and even researchers enthusiastic about the technology acknowledge that true translation remains a distant goal.

For now, AI may be less of a universal pet translator than an exceptionally attentive listener - one capable of spotting patterns across thousands of barks, whines and meows that humans might otherwise miss.
And until a machine can reliably tell you what your cat is thinking, experience suggests the answer will often remain familiar: “I want food!”
b1b7355af7a678e7: “Of all the gin joints, in all the towns in all the world…”
It had to be Anfield.
Manchester City must feel like Rick in Casablanca when they play their first match after the guilty verdict.
The fixture list shows a wicked sense of humour with Liverpool more than happy to be the femme fatale on this occasion.
We can be sure City would have preferred a home tie after such an apocalyptic ruling.
And, if not, anywhere but at the club that suffered the most from their serial cheating.
‘Hostile’ does not begin to describe the welcome they’re guaranteed to receive.
Anything between “a bear pit” and “a cauldron of hate” is what City can expect when they take the field on Sunday night (Malaysian time).
Anfield was simmering at the best of times, and City’s bus was attacked en route to the ground on one occasion.
You suspect the route will be a closely guarded secret this weekend, but as soon as it's spotted, the players can expect an eventful ride.
If that doesn’t shake them, the reception on the pitch will sort the men from the boys.
You have to feel a bit sorry for them, most of whom have been at the club for less than two years, and even the seniors cannot be blamed for the sins of their owners.
They can, though, be guilty of receiving “stolen goods”.
But it’s the head honchos, the plotters and the schemers, who should face football’s collective wrath.
People like chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak, who told UEFA when previously charged that they would sue for the next decade.
And what about Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan himself, who has only ever attended one Premier League game at the Etihad?
At least it would show some cojones if he turned up for this one.
Judging by City’s bullish response so far, it seems that they still don’t get it.
And if they put the warmth of Sunday’s “welcome” down to historic rivalry, they may be surprised to find hostility on every English ground they visit. And maybe a few foreign ones, too.
Let’s face it, City have cheated Europe as well.
And Liverpool fans are already saying they’ve never had so many fans of other clubs wanting them to win on Sunday.
Gary Neville puts it like this: “If City want to understand how angry the football world is, then Anfield will tell them in a way you would never believe.
“There will be banners, there will be chants, it will be a brutal day for them.”
Perhaps only then will the £900 million’s worth of pennies begin to drop.
City’s conniving and dishonest owners have turned a famous club into the pariahs of football, with every club suffering under the weight of their chicanery.
Liverpool came off worst, having had a likely golden era fall victim to blatant larceny.
Titles pinched. Winnings embezzled. Glory stolen.
Three times, they were pipped to the EPL title by fine margins, just 11 millimetres being the difference in 2019.
A rule-breaking £900 million of “disguised funding” was the real difference.
Not just football fans will be watching to see how this plays out.
City has reported that staff have been abused in the street. New players are bewildered and have their agents poring over their contracts.
You would love to know who had relegation clauses inserted.
They’ve had three weeks of international break to digest this, but it cannot have gone down very well.
Enzo Maresca has been defiant, as has Pep Guardiola, who is promising to attend the PSG game at the Etihad on Wednesday.
Most City fans will rally behind the team whose best bet seems to be to acquire “a siege mentality” because that’s how the season is going to feel.
They had started so well, winning every game to top the table. The match at Liverpool always stood out as a potential cracker with Andoni Iraola’s side still waiting for a spark.
Sunday’s atmosphere and City’s vulnerability could provide it.
Jeremy Jacquet looks a gem of a signing and with kids like Rio Ngumoha and Trey Nyoni coming through, the prospects look brighter on Merseyside.
If Cody Gakpo and Alexis Mac Allister can maintain their recent improvements, a decent season is in prospect.
But Florian Wirtz remains an enigma. His last season at Bayer Leverkusen saw him tot up 31 goal involvements. Last season at Liverpool, he got 18.
Although he scored a good goal for Jurgen Klopp’s Germany in the break, he still didn’t look like his old self.
At least Alexander Isak is beginning to resemble the striker Newcastle once had.
When you look at City and see the glittering array of exciting talent they have, the swindle makes you even more angry.
It would have been fascinating to see if they could challenge Arsenal, with many neutrals favouring City because they’re a much better watch.
But no more: from now on, the view is bound to be jaundiced.
We will not know where we stand until the appeal has been heard and probably well beyond that.
It’s unthinkable that the verdict can be overturned – English football would be a laughing stock.

So we have to hope that appropriate punishment is dished out soon. A points deduction to relegate them at least two divisions, a transfer ban and a monumental fine to be distributed to the rest of the league, including the EFL, is just the minimum for what is a crime against football.
In the meantime, clubs will show how they feel, starting with Liverpool on Sunday.

4957e3561ca0894c: From the Tengku Ampuan of Pahang, Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah
It began with a photograph of a boat-shaped formation and a simple question.
If the Qur’an tells us that the Ark of Prophet Nuh عليه السلام came to rest upon al-Judi, why do so many modern reports of its supposed discovery direct our attention towards Mount Ararat?

I found myself looking at maps, comparing mountains and imagining an expedition equipped with modern scanners. At one point, I laughingly suggested walking from one mountain to the other. With hundreds of kilometres between them, perhaps I should begin by finding better walking shoes. We might return with an article and very sore feet.
But beneath the laughter was a question worth pursuing. As a Muslim, my starting point is the Qur’an.
In Surah Hud, verse 44, Allah tells us:
وَاسْتَوَتْ عَلَى الْجُودِيِّ
“The Ark rested on Mount Judi.”
The name al-Judi therefore enters this inquiry through revelation. It does not originate in a modern expedition or a desire to challenge the popularity of Ararat.

The classical tafsir tradition gives us a starting point for understanding it. In his commentary on this verse, Ibn Kathir records explanations from early authorities, including Mujahid’s identification of al-Judi as a mountain in al-Jazirah, in Upper Mesopotamia. These accounts belong to the history of Muslim interpretation; their individual details still require appropriate assessment.
Here, an essential distinction emerges: the Qur’an’s naming of al-Judi is one matter; identifying its precise position on a modern map is another.

The mountain traditionally identified with al-Judi is Cudi Dağı, near Cizre in southeastern Turkey. That longstanding identification deserves examination, but it should not be presented as though modern coordinates were supplied by the Qur’an itself.
What, then, of Ararat?

Genesis refers to the “mountains of Ararat,” rather than explicitly naming the particular summit now commonly called Mount Ararat. Ararat is historically associated with Urartu, an ancient region and kingdom. The attachment of the biblical expression to today’s famous mountain developed through later traditions.
Could ancient geographical traditions concerning Judi and Ararat have overlapped in ways no longer obvious on a modern map?
It is a question requiring historical and geographical investigation. Similarities, differences and possible connections must be examined rather than assumed.

My article does not need to harmonise the two names. Nor does their difference, by itself, establish that a particular biblical passage was altered. We must distinguish the wording of a text from the interpretations and locations subsequently attached to it.

For a Muslim, the Qur’an remains the religious authority. Belief in Allah’s books and His messengers forms part of the six articles of faith, the Rukun Iman. We believe in the Taurat revealed to Musa, the Zabur to Daud, the Injil to Isa, and the Qur’an revealed to Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon them. Surah al-Nisa, verse 136, affirms belief in the revelation sent to the Prophet and in that sent before him.

This belief does not require us to identify every statement in the present biblical texts with the original revelations bestowed by Allah. The Injil mentioned in the Qur’an should not simply be equated with the collected writings of the New Testament, nor should the present text of Genesis be described without qualification as the original Taurat.

The Qur’an describes itself as confirming earlier scripture and as muhaymin over it, a guardian or criterion. Earlier texts may therefore be examined as historical and textual material without being assigned the same religious authority as the Qur’an.
My curiosity about these accounts arises within my Muslim faith. It also requires care in how I describe them.

We should not say that all four books contain an explicit narrative of the Ark. Genesis provides a detailed account, the New Testament recalls Noah and his vessel, and Psalms contains a possible allusion to the Flood. These are different kinds of reference.

Yet even as we examine the texts and maps, we must remember why the Qur’an tells us the story of Nuh. Its purpose is not to provide an excavation plan. Its lessons concern iman, tawhid, obedience, the consequences of rejecting revelation, and Allah’s power and mercy.

At the conclusion of this account in Surah Hud, verse 49, the Prophet is directed towards patience and the ultimate outcome for the righteous. The narrative leads us towards reflection and conduct, beyond curiosity about a mountain.
There is room for historical investigation. There is also a need to keep its claims within the limits of the evidence.

Gertrude Bell visited the mountain traditionally identified with Judi in 1909 and documented its landscape and the traditional site associated with the Ark. Friedrich Bender later reported collecting wood there. Their records concern journeys, investigations and inherited traditions. They do not establish that the Ark was found.

I also find myself wondering about remembrance. Would those who survived not have told their children about their deliverance? Might memories have endured in stories, place names and places of pilgrimage?
Kota Gelanggi comes to my mind when I consider how a place can remain alive in inherited stories while its location becomes a subject of inquiry. Such accounts deserve attentive listening.

But remembering an event and preserving its precise location are different things. Communities move, settlements disappear and names change. Oral traditions can guide questions; they must still be examined alongside written and material evidence.
Before we scan beneath the ground, perhaps we should first listen to the people who have lived upon it.

The boat-shaped formation at Durupınar, near Ararat, raises another set of questions. Supporters of the Ark hypothesis describe underground scan patterns resembling corridors or chambers. Those interpretations require verification, while published geological research has explained the formation as a natural structure.

Even if artificial chambers were established, what would prove that they belonged to a vessel? Could they belong to a building or a fortification? The thought crossed my mind, but it remains a possibility to test, not a finding.
A signal beneath the ground is the beginning of a question, not the answer. Ancient wood, an unusual outline or an apparent compartment cannot, on its own, identify the Ark of Nuh.
Our position can be expressed simply:
نُصَدِّقُ بِمَا جَاءَ فِي الْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ، وَنَتَوَقَّفُ فِيمَا لَا دَلِيلَ عَلَيْهِ.
“We affirm what has come in the Qur’an and Sunnah, and we withhold judgment concerning what has no evidence.”
We should be firm where revelation is firm, cautious where evidence is uncertain, and unwilling to turn speculation into certainty.
Our belief in the truth of the Qur’an does not depend upon archaeological verification. An expedition’s success or failure cannot determine that belief.

I began with two mountains and an imagined walk between them. I ended with a deeper appreciation of the need to distinguish revelation from geographical reconstruction, inherited tradition from established evidence, and curiosity from certainty.
The Ark of Nuh is a subject we may investigate. Its Qur’anic lessons are also lessons we must take to heart.

Faith brought me to the question. Curiosity led me to the map. Whether the mountains ever surrender their secret, the search must be conducted with humility, faithful to revelation and honest about the limits of our evidence.

Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah holds a master’s degree from the International Institute of Islamic Thought and Civilisation (ISTAC), International Islamic University Malaysia, and is currently a PhD candidate at ISTAC-IIUM.
605b9f635107c125: WASHINGTON: The vaccine skeptic US health secretary Robert Kennedy Jr announced Thursday a series of initiatives to study the rare adverse effects of vaccines.

"We must listen to patients and families who report vaccine injuries - not dismiss or gaslight them," Kennedy said in a statement announcing the creation of a research centre dedicated to monitoring and addressing vaccine side effects.

Appointed by president Donald Trump despite a lack of formal medical training, Kennedy has faced criticism from the World Health Organization (WHO) and other medical experts for efforts to overhaul child vaccinations in the United States.
Like all medicines, vaccines can have side effects, including mild ones such as slight fever or pain at the injection site.
Serious adverse effects remain very rare and are subject to continuous monitoring by health officials to ensure that vaccine benefits outweigh the risks.
According to WHO, vaccination currently prevents up to five million deaths every year from diseases such as diptheria, tetanus, influenza and measles.

"The issue really isn't whether we should study vaccine safety," epidemiologist Michael Osterholm, director of the University of Minnesota's Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy, told National Public Radio.
"Of course we should, but we already have systems in place that are constantly monitoring... to determine: Are there any adverse events associated with vaccination?"

Kennedy said the latest effort would help build a health system that "follows the evidence, and uses what we learn to make vaccines safer. This is how we earn back trust in our public health institutions."
The announcement comes as the federal health department has undergone significant budget cuts and the country faces its worst measles outbreak in 35 years.
The highly contagious illness has made a strong comeback in the US in recent years among unvaccinated populations, where growing mistrust of health officials has been reported.
In the eastern US state of Pennsylvania, local authorities have reported five measles-related deaths in 2026 alone.
54fba10c4a280491: Russian web giant Yandex says one of its cloud availability zones is unavailable due to a drone attack. Yandex is Russia’s rough equivalent of Google, and dominates the local market for search, email, and mapping services. The company also operates a cloud computing service whose status page says its ru-central1-b availability zone is down. “The incident was caused by a fire caused by a drone attack on Yandex's data center in Sasovo, which affected part of the Yandex Cloud infrastructure. Data center operations have been completely halted.” Sasovo is a town around 300 kilometers southeast of Moscow. Yandex later recommended users employ unspecified “alternative service restoration plans,” including its own bare metal servers, but advised users “it will not be possible to restore service in the near future.” The Russian company hasn’t commented on the source of the drone attack, but Ukrainian press report that President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Russia has attacked Ukrainian datacenters and that his government always responds in kind. Reuters reports that Yandex is uncertain if it is possible to restore operations at the datacenter. If Yandex must write off the datacenter, it will be the second cloud provider to lose facilities to drone attacks this year after AWS decided its Bahrain facility could not be recovered after an Iranian drone attack. Iran hit AWS facilities because it believed the cloud giant hosts workloads for the US military and its suppliers, and that an attack could therefore disrupt hostilities. For years, industry execs have told The Register that datacenters are critical infrastructure and will therefore likely become a target for kinetic attacks during conflict – either directly or by attacking their connections to energy grids and communications services. Clouds and pundits alike advise using multiple geographically dispersed availability zones, and cloud suppliers, to improve resilience. That advice is a little less potent in Russia, where sanctions mean local businesses aren’t welcome in clouds across the border. Russia also has a smaller pool of cloud operators to choose from. ®

4826f614ae9ee89e: KUALA LUMPUR: Every possible RM100 increase in minimum wage could cut consumer companies' earnings by up to 2.7 per cent, according to analysts.
They also said a minimum wage hike will strengthen household incomes and domestic demand without fuelling significant inflation.
Kenanga Research said a minimum wage increase could cut consumer-sector earnings by 0.1-2.7 per cent for every RM100 rise.
However, the firm noted that stronger household incomes could provide some offset.
Kenanga Research said the impact would be differentiated across the sector.
Labour-intensive companies are likely to face greater cost pressures while benefiting from potentially stronger consumer spending.
"Consumer spending has a cushion, but not without headwinds," Kenanga Research said in a note.
The firm said household purchasing power should remain supported by targeted fiscal assistance such as Sumbangan Asas Rahmah and Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah, as well as potentially higher wages.
However, companies are entering a less favourable cost environment as labour, electricity, freight and selected input costs rise.
Price-sensitive consumers could also limit companies' ability to pass higher costs on to customers, putting further pressure on margins.
BIMB Securities sees a potential RM2,000 minimum wage as supportive of household incomes and domestic demand, saying it would make the benefits of economic growth more inclusive.
It said Malaysia's median monthly salary had risen steadily from about RM1,500 in 2010 to RM2,957 in 2025, broadly alongside successive minimum wage increases from RM900 in 2013 to RM1,700 in 2025.

BIMB Securities said previous minimum wage increases had not triggered significant inflationary pressures, with median salaries rising faster than both the consumer price index and producer price index.
It said food inflation remained the main driver of cost-of-living pressures, with food accounting for about 30 per cent of the CPI basket.
As such, a potential RM2,000 minimum wage would be more likely to boost incomes than trigger a sharp rise in inflation, it said.
Young workers are expected to be among the biggest beneficiaries, with median earnings for those aged 15 to 19 projected at about RM1,899 in 2026, below the proposed threshold.

BIMB Securities said raising the minimum wage to RM2,000 in 2027 could give workers in that age group an immediate 5.3 per cent increase in median earnings, while strengthening incentives to join the workforce.
However, the impact would remain uneven across industries, particularly in labour-intensive manufacturing.

BIMB Securities said sectors such as apparel, food processing, footwear, fabricated metal products and transport equipment employ a large share of lower-wage workers earning below or near the proposed threshold.
These segments could face greater labour cost pressures, potentially squeezing margins unless offset by productivity gains, automation or higher value-added production.

The firm said Malaysia's broader labour market generally showed a positive relationship between productivity and wages, with manufacturing, construction and services recording productivity gains alongside rising wages.

On balance, BIMB Securities said a potential RM2,000 minimum wage was consistent with Malaysia's broader objective of raising labour income, strengthening domestic demand and moving towards a higher-income economy.
It said near-term margin pressure on labour-intensive sectors could remain manageable if accompanied by productivity-enhancing investments and labour market reforms.
Meanwhile, Kenanga Research sees another potential headwind from overnight policy rate (OPR) normalisation, forecasting a possible 25-basis-point hike in the first quarter of 2027.
Historically, consumer sentiment and share prices weakened following two of the three previous OPR hiking cycles.
The firm said companies that can capture resilient consumption without taking on disproportionate cost pressures should be better positioned.
Despite the challenges, Kenanga Research remains "Overweight" on the consumer sector, saying many concerns have been increasingly reflected in valuations following recent share price weakness.
It favours companies with defensive demand, manageable cost exposure and better earnings visibility, with QL Resources Bhd as its top pick, rated "Outperform" with a target price of RM4.40.

a144b5e9db3bbe41: WELCOMING a new member of staff is about much more than showing them where to sit, explaining their responsibilities and handing them a list of tasks.

The first few days can shape how a person feels about an organisation, their colleagues and their own place within the team. A thoughtful welcome can make someone feel valued, respected and confident from the very beginning.
The first step is to make sure their arrival is expected. Nothing makes a new employee feel more uncomfortable than arriving to find that nobody knows who they are or why they are there.
Their workspace, equipment and any necessary paperwork should be ready. Someone should also be available to greet them personally and introduce them to the people they will be working with.
A warm introduction matters. Rather than simply saying someone's name and moving on, take a moment to explain who they are and what they will be doing.

Encourage existing members of staff to welcome them properly. Small gestures, such as offering them a cup of tea or inviting them to join the team for lunch, can make a surprisingly significant difference.
A new member of staff will naturally have many questions. Some will be about their role, while others may seem insignificant to an experienced employee.
They may wonder where to find certain things, who to approach when they need help, how breaks work or even where they are expected to eat lunch.
These questions should never be dismissed. What seems obvious to someone who has been there for years may be completely unfamiliar to a newcomer.
Being patient and approachable creates an environment where the new employee feels comfortable asking for help rather than being afraid of making mistakes.
It is also important to explain the wider picture. A person needs to understand not only what they are expected to do, but why their contribution matters.
Explain the organisation's values, expectations and objectives in simple terms. Show them how their role connects with the work of other people.
This helps a new employee see themselves as part of something bigger.
They are not simply completing a list of duties. They are contributing to a team, and their work has a purpose.
Introducing colleagues properly is another important part of the process.

A new employee should know who they will be working with and who they can approach for different types of support. Where possible, introductions should include a little context rather than simply names and job titles.
For example, explaining that a particular colleague is the person who normally helps with a certain process gives the newcomer useful information and an immediate point of contact.
It also creates opportunities for relationships to develop naturally.
A new member of staff should also be given time to settle in. There is often a temptation to provide too much information during the first day.
However, people cannot absorb everything at once. Important information should be introduced gradually and reinforced over time.
Clear expectations are equally important. The employee should understand their responsibilities, priorities and standards, but they should not be expected to know everything immediately.
Give them realistic objectives for their first few days and weeks. As their confidence grows, responsibilities can increase.

A good manager should check in regularly during the early stages. This does not mean constantly watching over someone. Instead, simple conversations can help identify questions, concerns or difficulties before they become problems.
Asking, "How are you settling in?" is useful, but more specific questions can be even better.
Asking what they have found clear, what they are still unsure about and whether they need anything can encourage a more honest conversation.
Making someone feel part of a team also requires inclusion. Invite the new employee to meetings and conversations that are relevant to their role.
Include them in social activities and informal discussions. Do not allow them to remain on the outside simply because they are new.
At the same time, inclusion should not mean forcing someone to participate in everything.
People have different personalities and levels of confidence. The aim is to create opportunities for connection without making the person feel uncomfortable.
Existing staff also have a role to play. A welcoming workplace is not created by one manager alone.
Everyone should understand that a new colleague may need patience, guidance and encouragement while they learn how things work.
Finally, remember that belonging develops over time. A successful welcome does not end after the first day or even the first week.
Continue to communicate, offer support and recognise progress. A simple word of encouragement can make a new employee feel that their efforts are noticed.

The best welcome is ultimately a human one. Treat the new member of staff with respect, give them the information and support they need, introduce them to their colleagues and allow them time to find their feet.
When people feel welcomed rather than merely employed, they are more likely to develop confidence, build strong relationships and become committed members of the team.
